Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 13 relating to the submission to parliament of certain regulations and orders in council.
Explain.

The Dominion Lands Act of 1906 contained provision for the tabling of orders in council. When the act was revised in 1908 provision was included that these orders in council tabled should be approved by resolution by both houses. The Forest Reserves and Parks Act, which was passed in 1911, contained similar provision. Orders in council under these acts are valid only for one day after the session closes unless they have previously been approved by each house of parliament. For several years the orders in council, although tabled, were not con- ' firmed by resolution, and in 1928 action was taken by special act of parliament, chap. 44, Geo. V. 18-19, assented to 11th June, 1928, validating the orders in council passed up to that time. The present bill is to validate the orders in council passed between the 7th December, 1929, and the 31st January, 1931, which have been tabled in both houses.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. HEAPS (North Winnipeg) moved:
subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
Whereas there are large and increasing numbers of our citizens at present unable to obtain employment and thereby the means of existence.
And whereas during recent years production has increased enormously.
And whereas real wages have not increased in proportion and thus consumption has not kept pace with production,
Be it resolved: that, in the opinion of this house, in order to absorb the unemployed into industry, thus eliminating the enormous waste of enforced idleness, the hours of labour be materially reduced and the purchasing power of the masses increased, and further to this end, that the government be requested to submit the necessary measures to the house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that during the course of the present session there will be submitted to this house legislation of a very important character. We will have before us matters concerning the railway situation and probably the great waterways of Canada, but to my mind there is at the present time no question of such vast importance to the people of this dominion as is that of unemployment. The other matters referred to sink into insignificance when compared with this great problem, this great tragedy, which is now stalking throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada. In my opinion it is time this parliament tackled most earnestly the problem of unemployment. So far there has been no inkling or no indication whatsoever as to what steps the government may take to meet existing conditions.
In 1930 the matter of unemployment became a vital issue in this house, and many times during the session the problem was 
discussed. At that time the party in opposition accepted the challenge, if they were returned to power, to deal with unemployment, and having accepted the challenge the electors of the Dominion of Canada sent them back to this house with a very large majority. The party now in power will ultimately be judged by its action in this connection. In 1930 when the Liberal party went to the country unemployment was a vital factor, and I do not think I am exaggerating in the slightest degree when I say it was one of the chief contributing factors in putting them where they are at the present time. If the Conservative party accepted the challenge in 1930-and I give them credit for having done so-I do not think I am asking for more than my just rights when in 1932 I ask them what they are going to do about this great problem of unemployment.
I realize fully the attempts they have made to deal with the matter; I realize that they have jacked up the tariff as high as possible; to a very large extent they have spent public moneys to provide public works; they have been giving relief on a vast scale to thousands and thousands of Canadians throughout the length and breadth of the dominion. On the one hand we find they have been giving concessions or doles to the manufacturers and on the other hand they have been giving doles to the people who are being deprived of the opportunity to work. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that doles, whether they be given to those at the top or those at the bottom, are not going to solve the problem of unemployment.
During the past year or so the problem has become considerably aggravated, and instead of conditions improving the opposite has been the case. For the last eighteen months the Conservative party has been in power, and those who are in close touch with the situation will realize the conditions existing to-day in many of our large industrial centres; at this time I shall not discuss what is happening in our rural areas. May I quote to hon. members just a few figures concerning the cities of Winnipeg and Montreal. On January 20 last, just a few brief weeks ago, in the city of Winnipeg there were 5,079 married men, heads of families, who were in receipt of public relief. At the same time there were 5,388 single men and 493 single women receiving similar aid. The best figure I have been able to obtain from authoritative sources in regard to the city of Winnipeg indicates that at the present time there are 20,000 men and women out of work.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps
This figure, may I add, does not include very large numbers of people who are at present engaged on relief work. If these people were taken into consideration the figure I have already given would be greatly increased.
Yesterday while in the city of Montreal I heard an alderman of that city discuss their unemployment situation. He stated that for a long time very little had been done to relieve conditions, and very little in the way of obtaining accurate data was being attempted. The situation became so acute that they decided to take a registration, and within a period of ten days over 19,000 heads of families registered as being willing to work with pick and shovel for approximately forty cents per hour. This figure does not include single men and thousands of others who would have registered had there been any prospects of employment for them. If we accept those figures as correct-and there is no doubt they are-then it means that there are in some of our large industrial centres from one-quarter to one-third of the workers actually either on relief or demanding measures to take care of them.
Undoubtedly we will be told that in Canada we are suffering from world conditions. I have no doubt that to a certain extent conditions prevailing in certain other parts of the world are reflected in Canada, but we as a Labour party are not going to accept the excuse that because there are bad conditions throughout the world the same are bound to exist here. If we in this dominion were short of the essentials or necessities of life I could quite understand there being some excuse on the part of the powers that be for the prevailing conditions. But we are not suffering from any famine condition, any shortage of the necessities of life; we are suffering, if anything, from a "famine of plenty."
Now, so far this session the only indication we have had of what .the government propose to do to deal with the problem is the announcement made by the Prime Minister a few days ago that the salaries of civil servants would be reduced by 10 per cent. I want to take this first opportunity of protesting on the floor of the house against this action. I would not have objected so much if the government had accepted the cost of living figures as submitted by the Department of Labour or the Bureau of Statistics, and then decided to make some minor reduction in the salaries of those in the civil service receiving the higher scales of pay; but the government simply announce that all civil servants wil-l have to submit to a reduction of 10 per cent in their salaries. [DOT]
I suppose this is one of the remedies the government are taking to cope with the present situation. Well, as representing a labour constituency and the ideals and aspirations of labour in parliament, I desire to contrast that action with another action the government took only a few short weeks ago. The government wanted money, and naturally they had to go to the capitalists to obtain it. What did they do? Did they say to our financiers: "You have got to accept a lower rate of interest for the money that we want you to loan to the government"? Oh, no. They went to our moneyed people and said: "If you will let us have your money we will give you a higher rate of interest than you have ever had in the history of this dominion." Had the government insisted on a lower rate of interest, the saving to the country would have been sufficient to have rendered unnecessary the 10 per cent salary reduction. In other words, the government are reducing the salaries of the workers in order that they may pay increased interest to the wealthy people of the dominion. In my view, this shows a complete lack of knowledge as to what the great masses of the people are thinking at the present time.
I propose to give a few figures as to interest charges, because they undoubtedly have a certain vital bearing upon the whole question of national economics. I am bringing these figures to the attention of the house because apparently so far the only government policy for dealing with the situation is the policy of "rigid economy", and I want to show where that policy might be applied. In 1914, prior to the war, the total fixed interest charges of the dominion were $12,893,505; the total revenue receipts were $163,174,000. In other words, our interest charges were a little over 8i peT cent of our total revenue receipts. But in 1931 those respective figures had increased to $121,289,844 and $356,209,358; that is, our percentage of interest charges to receipts had gone up from 8-6 to 32 per cent. Putting it another way, while our revenue had increased about 150 per cent, our interest charges had increased over 1,000 per cent. I submit that if the government were determined upon a policy of rigid economy that is where the saving might have been started.
The test part of my motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, in order to absorb the unemployed into industry, thus eliminating the enormous waste of enforced idleness, the hours of labour be materially reduced and the purchasing power of the masses increased

With the vast number of people that we have out of work, I think the first question I
186	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps
ought to submit to this house is:	How are
those people going to be absorbed into industry? The fact is that to-day they cannot be so absorbed, otherwise they would be working. That being so, I think I ought to submit to the house some concrete proposals as to the measures that should be taken to that end. It has been stated, and I think, correctly so, that there is only one cure for unemployment, that is to provide work. If to-day the panaceas offered to parliament for the cure of unemployment have proven ineffective, then I think it is only right and proper that we should turn to other measures for dealing with this very serious problem.
During the past few years production in Canada has increased by leaps and bounds. I do not think there is any doubt about that, and I do not think it is necessary for me to quote statistics in support of my statement. It will be sufficient for my purpose to state that according to the figures submitted by the Bureau of Statistics, during the period from 1917 to 1929 there was an increase in production of over 70 per cent. During approximately the same period, between 1917 and 1928, real wages, that is, wages as measured in terms of purchasing power, have increased by 16-4 per cent. In other words, productivity has increased beyond all proportion to the increase in wages. So long as we have this tremendous spread between the wages received and the value produced, I submit there is no hope of solving the problem of unemployment. During that same period of about eleven years, according to the Bureau of Statistics, the number of wage earners in Canada increased from 552,968 to 566,780-an increase of only 13,812; or to put it another way, individual production increased by an enormous ratio, while wages increased by a very small ratio. In 1928 the average amount of production per person employed in industry in Canada was $5,729; in other words, every man and woman in the dominion working in industry produced this value in commodities; but the amount received back in the form of wages was only $1,024 per person. This figure, however, does not tell the whole story in regard to labour costs; I think there should be other items added to the $1,024, because I am confident there are some missing. But at the same time there is another aspect of this question that in my opinion will compensate for any omissions from $1,024, because it should be borne in mind that the figure of $5,729 as the amount produced by every person working in industry represents the value of the goods when they leave the gates of the manufac-

turers. By the time those goods reach the consumer their price perhaps has doubled, so if there is anything lacking in the computation of labour costs probably it would be compensated for by the increase in price of the commodities which the worker has to buy back from the retail stores.
From this it will be seen, Mr. Speaker, that those who come in between the man who produces and the consumer are taking far too large a toll of the goods or the wealth of this country. We in the Labour party claim, as I believe many of those belonging to other groups in this house also claim, that unless that spread is decreased there is no hope of dealing with the problems of poverty and unemployment with which we are now faced.
If we are to deal with this question at all I think first we must see that the people have access to the commodities which they produce. At the present time they have not that access, because in the first place they have not the purchasing power, and they have not that purchasing power because they do not receive sufficient in the form of wages. So we claim that one thing we must do is see that the people get more in the form of wages than they receive at the present time. But, as I said a moment ago, if we are to absorb more people into industry, how can that be accomplished? To-day we can produce far more rapidly than we are allowed to consume, and in fact I believe I am correct when I say that we can produce far more rapidly than we could consume even if we were allowed to consume a reasonable amount. If that is the case there is no problem of production; we have more or less solved that problem. So it comes down to a question of distribution, and I think the problem facing parliament at present is how to bring about a more equitable distribution of the wealth produced.
If we are to absorb more people into industry I think that can only be done in one way. There is no use talking of markets in other parts of the world; every other country is attempting to find those markets, and all the nations of the world cannot be on an export basis. So if we are to provide work for all those who want work I think that can be done only by reducing the hours of labour so that more people may be employed, and a matter of this kind can be dealt with only through the federal parliament; it cannot be done by provincial legislation. That is why I am asking the federal government to take the initiative in legislation of that nature.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps
Then we come to the question of the distribution of the commodities and the wealth produced. I submit that this question of distribution can be solved only in part by increasing the purchasing power of the masses of the people, and that can be brought about only by giving those who are performing useful service a greater return in the form of real wages than they are receiving at the present time. The figures I have submitted to the house show that at present approximately one-fifth of the value of an article is paid to the persons engaged in its production in the form of wages, and perhaps if other charges are taken into consideration that proportion might increase to one-quarter. The man engaged in industry can repurchase only one-quarter of the commodities which he produces, and the rest must wait until an export market is found or until it is consumed in one way or another.
I believe an increasing number of people favour the idea of shorter hours. This is not prevalent only among those who belong to the Labour -party; we find that opinion held by many belonging to other parties, and I was very much interested a short time ago in the statement of a gentleman who is well known to members of this house. Speaking in Toronto he said:
Unless inventive genius can devise new services or industries to absorb the present machine created surplus of workers, the nations of the world must unite in a pact to reduce *working hours. . . .
That statement was made by the present leader of the Senate, and I am wondering whether the leader of the Conservative party in this house will accept that dictum. I thought the leader of the Senate was getting to the stage where he might soon join the Labour party, but when I learned that he had been made leader of the Senate I felt that my party had lost a possible recruit.
I think I have quoted enough figures to show that at present too large a proportion is going to sources that neither toil nor spin, I find, Mr. Speaker, that during 1931 the amount paid in the Dominion of Canada in the form of dividends totalled a large sum. The year 1931 was disastrous for millions of people in Canada; in that year hundreds of thousands of our fellow-Ganadians lived on relief; farmers were on the verge of poverty, unable to meet their obligations; thousands of workers in our cities were going to relief offices in the hope of being able -to obtain something in the way of -assistance. But wha-t do we find? In 1929 the total amount paid in dividends, according to the Montreal Star of December 16, 1931, was $215,097,291, while
in the -poor year of 1931 the amount paid in dividends and profits was $210,221,919, or a difference of approximately $5,000,000.
From this I -think it must be obvious that to-day profits are levying too great a toll upon industry, and it must be apparent that instead of going to the few these profits should go to the many. It may be asked how this is to be -brought about, and I must say frankly that in my opinion the only way to make the changes I have briefly enumerated this afternoon is to bring in state regulation to a greater extent than is the case at present.
I know some hon. members Shudder at the idea of state regulation, but there is no need to be afraid of the term. To-day the state interferes in practically everything we do. Every time there is a tariff change in this house it means some form of state interference with business, and if we can interfere with business for the purpose of putting it on a stable foundation I think in these times there is no reason why we should not interfere in order to put the living conditions of the masses of the people on a firm foundation as well.
When I bring this question to the attention of parliament my mind goes back to the scenes I witnessed in my own city of Winnipeg a few weeks ago before I left for Ottawa. There I saw thousands of single men being fed. They were trooping into buildings and warehouses where hundreds at a time sat down to a rather skimpy meal which they received from the city through the fund provided for the purpose by the three public authorities. There they sat down, and amongst those men we can find some of the flower of our manhood. These men, when wanted during the year 1914, became the nation's heroes, and in 1932 they have become the nation's hoboes. They come from all walks of -life: you will find among them the ordinary labourer as well as mechanics skilled and unskilled, yes, and even lawyers and doctors, all receiving relief. When in the city of Winnipeg at the present time between one-quarter and one-third of the population are in receipt of some form of public assistance, I ask this House of Commons : How long can a condition of that kind continue? Here we have come to parliament and so far we find not a word said about this serious problem of unemployment. I know it is still early in the session, but not a thing has been foreshadowed to meet the situation. The workers, the great masses of the people in the country, are to-day looking to parliament to do something to deal in a fundamental way with this great and very important problem.
1S8	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gershaw
Right at this moment while this matter is being discussed in the House of Commons there are doubtless hundreds of thousands of workers, affected by the problem, who are wondering what steps the government will take to cope with the situation. I trust this afternoon that the government will take the present opportunity to tell the house and the country what they have in mind in this regard. When we realize that to-day in our midst there are hundreds of thousands who month after month have been living on some form of dole we can well believe that the people are looking to parliament to give them a lead. They want some assurance. These people are being driven deeper and deeper into the mire, with the result that they are beginning to lose their manhood and womanhood, to-day we ought to give them a message not merely of hope and encouragement but of something practical in the way of an assurance that the government and parliament are going to tackle in a real and earnest manner this greatest of all problems that we have had to face.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
1 will not take up the time of the house trying to make it clear that there is a great unemployment problem in Canada to-day. The question of the reduction of working hours is a very old one, but to-day, owing to changed economic conditions, it must be viewed in rather a new light. In past years, before factories reached their present state of productive efficiency, the effect of overstrain, through long hours, upon the health of the individual and the question as to how the hours of leisure would be spent were all important. These problems have been largely dealt with and to-day the whole subject must be approached from the point of view of trying to some extent to solve the great problem of unemployment which is so much in evidence.
Stephen Leacock said in 1921 that the power of workers to produce had increased fortyfold in the past 150 years. Since that time inventors have developed many other laboursaving devices:	We have combines displacing labour in the harvest field; we have powerful engines pulling long freight trains and so displacing the number of crews previously employed; and we have in the factory labour-saving devices through the operation of which only a small fraction of the number of men previously employed can now obtain work. It has happened before, when this problem became serious, that a war or something of that kind would occur and thousands

of men were absorbed into armies, navies and other services. We do hope that such a thing will not be needed to relieve the present situation; we hope that instead of more armaments we shall have less as time goes on. In the past also more work has been available during periods of construction when branch railways were being built to open up new territories, and when building materials to construct homes, stores and elevators were required, and when there was at least a temporary market for machinery and requisite material of every kind. Then much work was available.
We heard a few days ago about one country that is trying a new experiment and we find that there they have no unemployment problem, probably because they are going through a period of construction. But in our country our plant has already been overbuilt; production has probably been overdone, and we find that thousands of men are laid off. This seems to work in a vicious circle. Men are laid off; there is no purchasing power; factories cannot sell their products, and more men are laid off. And so the vicious circle goes round and round. We also have boys and girls who are growing up in the country and there is little prospect of their obtaining work under present conditions. Can anything be more unfortunate than to see an aged, infirm man having to go out and work with pick and shovel while some of his grownup boys, unmarried, are out of work and unable to give him any help. During recent years hours of labour have been shortened. The figures show that from 1913 to 1926 hours of labour dropped 20 per cent and it was predicted at that time that disaster would follow. But that prediction has not been justified. Shorter hours of labour, it is true, would increase factory costs, but can that be avoided? Has not the cost of unemployment to be met in any case? If, therefore, factory costs might be slightly increased it would probably in the end result in a saving to the taxpayers of Canada.
I am in favour of this resolution. I believe it would work in the interests of the Canadian people. It would make for contentment because it would give a wider distribution of the available amount of work and a wider distribution of the wealth available in the country; and if the economic interests of the few clash with the wellbeing of the many, then surely the latter must have the preference. I believe that by shortening the hours of work some progress would be made in solving the great unemployment problem.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. MacNicol

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
I desire to pass a few comments on
this resolution but I hope that the mover (Mr. Heaps) will not gather from anything that I say that I contemplate associating myself with the Labour party. The remarks I make I make from the point of view of one who has been inside the walls of industry for approximately a quarter of a century, looking out on the world from that aspect, not looking in through the windows and telling those inside what to do and the men in there how they are to conduct themselves. I propose to confine myself largely to the resolution.
In connection with production, if we take the index in Canada as of 1913-and I believe they use 1913 in both Canada and the United States as the basis of their index figures- but if we bring the index figure down to 1926 and accept 100 as the index for that year, we find that production in Canada advanced from 1926 to the peak in January, 1929, when it reached 43 points higher than normal, or the index rose to 143. From 1929 to December, 1931, the index lowered and lowered as far as productivity in Canada is concerned, until in December, 1931, it stood at 82. Therefore the statement in the resolution as far as increased production is concerned, must refer to 1929, the high-water mark, because since that time, as I have said, there has been a consistent contraction of business.
With reference to wages, if we take the real wages also as of the period of 1926, what do we find? Using the figures which have been assembled by the Department of Labour in Canada-I do not know whether they are issued yet-we shall first take actual wages as of 1926 at 100, the cost of living at 100, and real wages at 100. There is a wide distinction between real wages and actual wages. Real wages means the amount that can be purchased by the actual money received in proportion to the prices of the commodities. In 1931, actual wages had risen from the index of 100 in 1926, to 106. The cost of living on the other hand, starting with 100 as the index in 1926, had decreased until in December, 1931, it stood at 89, or eleven points below normal. Actual wages, as I said a moment ago, stood in December, 1931, at six points above normal, if we assume 1926 as normal. Real wages figured on that basis in December, 1931, stood at 119. I merely leave those figures with the members, and I shall pass on to the next item.
The resolution refers to the reduction in the hours of labour. At the present time many thousands of men and women are out of work, and we cannot reduce their hours
of labour. Many more thousands are working on part time, and their hours of labour should not be reduced. Even those who are working full time are compelled to make voluntary contributions from their incomes and this is equivalent to shortening their hours also. The application of the principle of shorter hours is not new. It commenced in 1840 when President Van Buren of the United States adopted the ten-hour day principle for all government services in that republic. The next move was in 1879 by the state legislature of Massachusetts when it adopted regulations pertaining to the hours of labour of women and shortened the period of work for women. Then in 1886 the movement commenced in Canada to have shorter hours of work; thus from 1840 to 1886 the period of hours of work was reduced. I am not a prophet, but I do not hesitate to say that in the future the hours of labour will be reduced still further than they are to-day.
There has been a tremendous advance in production. The leaders of industry and likewise the leaders of the different labour organizations have taken careful note of that. How could there be anything but an advance in industry when we consider there has been a tremendous advance in chemistry, physics and the science of mathematics? If we take into consideration the application to industry of the advances in those educational fields, naturally production did increase and by 1929 the productivity of the plants in America exceeded the productivity in 1919 by approximately fifty per cent. That is, the productivity of every man engaged in industry in 1929, owing to the improvement in the machines in the industry in which he worked, and applying this generally to industries, increased fifty per cent.
The very fact that machines have improved so that the productivity has increased, has resulted in numerous surveys, at all times encouraged by those engaged in industry, both the employers and the workmen. The first survey was made in 1908 by the National Industrial Congress Board of New York. They endeavoured to ascertain if the number of days per week for work had been reduced in a number of United States plants, and they found in 1908 that eight plants in that country had reduced the work per week from six to five days. In 1931, last year, the United States Labour department made a much wider and more extended investigation. Their questionnaire covered 37,587 companies and they ascertained that those companies employed approximately 4,000,000 men or women as the case might be. They learned in reply
190	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. MacNicol
to the questionnaire that 892 of those companies had adopted the five-day week as a permanent principle in their plants. If we apply the percentage to the numbers engaged, we find that approximately 225,000 of the
4,000,000 were permanently on the five-day week.
Later on, just last year, I believe, the Industrial Standards Board of New York sent out a questionnaire to 2,000 firms in the United States. This questionnaire was replied to by 266 firms. The questions were:
1.	Are you in favour of a shorter week?
2.	Are you in favour of fewer hours per day?
In reply to the first question, "Are you in favour of a shorter work week?" fifty-three per cent of the firms replied no, and forty-six per cent firms replied yes. I am leaving out the decimals. In reply to the second question, "Are you in favour of fewer hours per day?" Thirty-six per cent of the firms replied yes, and sixty-three per cent of the firms replied no.
The experience of the Kellogg Company of Battle Creek, Michigan, I believe will be of interest in this connection. The Kellogg Company in December, 1930, went on a shorter shift schedule. They operate twenty-four hours per day and they divided the work into four shifts of six hours each. That resulted in their adding to their staff three hundred more operators. I should just like to quote a few sentences from what they say as to the results as printed in the October issue of Factory and Industrial Management. These were the advantages for the employees: More leisure time for recreation.
Opportunity to cultivate gardens.
Time to pursue educational courses.
Increased incentive to prepare for managerial jobs.
Less fatigue, resulting in a more healthy, ambitious, alert and aggressive working force.
Opportunity for mothers who must support children to earn a living and yet have ample time at home to care for their families.
Less waste time, due to concentration of work in a single period.
Decreased cost of living-all meals at home.
Now as to the company itself. The advantages according to this article have been as follows:
Increased daily production from the plants as an operating unit, due to increased production at every station or task, slight in itself, but considerable in the aggregate.
Elimination of meal periods, with their waste and the expense of a large cafeteria.
As most hon. gentlemen know, nearly all the larger industries maintain cafeterias which supply meals for their employees. I continue to quote:

Increased return from the capital invested in plant and machinery, owing to the increased rate of plant operation.
Decreased overhead due to the fact that the factory produces more packages of cereals per dollar of overhead than under the eight-hour shifts.
I should also like to quote from a book published by the National Industrial Conference Board, New York, entitled The Five-Day Week in Manufacturing Industries. A very close study was made of this question of the shorter working week in the state of New York, and I should like to quote a few sentences from the conclusions of these investigators. They say:
The conclusion that any or all industrial establishments could advantageously adopt the five-day week schedule does not follow from the evidence offered in its favour by a majority of the companies that are qualified from experience to appraise its advantages and drawbacks. This evidence does, however, remove the five-day week from the status of a radical and impractical administrative experiment.
Whether or not the application of the five-day week will be extended to industry generally, and whether such extension would be economically sound and socially desirable, are questions that lie in the field of conjecture and opinion and are outside the scope of this study.
In the end, the question of the length and arrangement of the working week is likely to be settled, not on the basis of theoretical principles, but by the practical experience of employers and workers, individually and in groups.
In this connection I would say that there are many lines of industry which cannot perhaps have a shorter working week, either shorter hours per day or fewer days per week. On the other hand I am told that in certain industries men are working seven days per week. So far as I am concerned, I would like to see that practice entirely eliminated if at all possible. I do not think anyone should work seven days a week if it can be avoided.
Next, if industry is to progress it is bound to take advantage of the benefits of invention, particularly along the lines to which I referred some moments ago in connection with chemistry, mathematics, physics and so forth, and of course these inventions may increase the difficulty in connection with employment.
I for one am convinced that a study such as is suggested in the resolution is worth while, and I was pleased to see the motion on the order paper because it directs public attention to the matter. While I do not think that anything can be done now, perhaps when the depression lifts and we get into good times again and industry bounds along, regulations may be made which will prove advantageous.
I am convinced that it will never do to allow

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
machinery to develop and continue to displace labour to a greater extent than it does to-day without some provision being made for the future. It will never do to deny to men the opportunity to work through machinery displacing labour. I can remember well When I was a boy many I knew worked twelve hours per day in industry. I have seen in my time the number of working hours per day reduced from twelve to ten, and from ten to nine. I believe that Canada along with other signatories to the Treaty of Versailles has agreed to place in operation at the earliest convenient time the eight-hour day. So there is no reason to think that a shorter working day will not come. Whether the time is ripe now, I do not know. Whether it is economically sound at the present time,
I cannot say. I rise merely to give my support to whatever will increase the demand for the services of workingmen, whatever will increase the opportunity for men to serve and increase the numbers that may be employed. The subject of employment in industry has been one of profound interest to me for many, many years, and I am happy at all times to do what I can in any way I can to provide men with the opportunity to work. If, when times get better, it is found necessary to reduce the hours of work and if such action increases the opportunity to serve, I think I will be in a position to advocate along that line.	[DOT]

I am pleased the hon.
member has asked the question. In Canada so far as I know at the present time no firms are operating on a five-day week basis. The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company of Canada, Limited, operating in Toronto is on a six-hour shift, four shifts per day. The Kellogg Company, to which I referred, operating on a six-hour shift, raised the wages of the men in the plant 33 1-3 per cent thereby making the wages from the six-hour day equivalent to those from the eight-hour day. In that plant the wages of the office staff were raised only 12| per cent because that staff was receiving higher salaries. I read a moment ago from Factory and Industrial Management in connection with the Kellogg Company. They were satisfied that even operating on the six-hour day costs were cut down and the production was as great.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to second the
resolution of the hon. member for North
Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) I wish to say I am pleased the resolution has come before the house so early in the session. During the session of last year hon. members in this corner of the house made every effort to promote a discussion of the unemployment situation throughout this dominion, and to have something done early in the session so that every opportunity would be given for discussion. However, we failed in that, and not until the closing day of the session was anything said concerning unemployment or remedies proposed by the government in regard thereto.
As the mover of the resolution has pointed out, in 1930 unemployment became a matter of national importance and an issue in the election of that year. I took the position at that time that the government of the day was not responsible for the prevailing economic conditions, and took the further position that the government which would succeed them, if there were a change, would not be able to deal effectively with unemployment because our economic system, as everyone knows who has given it any thought, is not carried out according to plan. It runs here and there where it will, according to the time and circumstances in which it finds itself, and for that reason I realize that the present government, regardless of their pre-election promises, cannot effectively deal with the problem. They made the promises, however, in 1930 and at the special session, with a great deal of confidence, they sought to work out a remedy. In the session of 1931 however they realized that their efforts were not going to be effective, and although they tried to do something further they began to draw attention to the fact that hon. members on this side of the house were not making any constructive suggestions toward a solution. What a constructive suggestion is or means depends on the definition of the term. If they mean a suggestion which would cure unemployment and improve industrial and social relations as between the various classes in this country, we say we cannot make such constructive suggestions because unemployment arises out of the relations existing between the different classes in Canada.
However I pointed out about a week after the session opened last year that one of the few ways in which the government could deal with unemployment was to reduce the hours of work and increase the wages of workers in industry. Unfortunately however that suggestion was not accepted; undoubtedly the government considered it was not constructive and, in the same manner, they may feel that

Unemployment Relie]-Mr. Maclnnis
the present resolution is of the same nature. Several points are made in the resolution now before us. First, there is the statement, in effect, that the condition of unemployment is becoming worse. I quote from the resolution as follows:
Whereas there are large and increasing numbers of our citizens at present unable to obtain employment and thereby the means of existence.
I do not think anyone denies that statement. If we turn to the Labour Gazette of January, 1932, however we will find therein ample proof of the statement made in this resolution. On page 56 I find the following: The curtailment in industrial activity, which first appeared towards the latter part of 1929 and continued throughout 1930, became more pronounced during the year just passed, with the result that employment in Canada was generally at a lower level during 1931 than in any other year since 1926.
Then, if we turn to page 57 we find a
chart describing the state of employment in Canada from the year 1921 to 1931, indicating that the peak of employment was reached about the middle of the year 1929. At that time, comparing with the figure 100 which is given for the year 1926, the peak is indicated at 127-8. From that time to the end of 1931, when the index figure is 98, we find a continuous decline in employment. When I say, "continuous" may I add that the term is interpreted in only one way, because there was an up trend in 1930 and a lesser up trend in 1931. Taking the main curve however there is shown to be a continuous decline since the middle of 1929. If we take the index figures of employment supplied to the Bureau of Statistics by the various employers in the dominion, taking the year 1926 as the average of 100, in 1930 the index reached its maximum of 118-9 on July 1, while the highest point reached in 1929 was 127-8 at the beginning of August. During the year under review the index averaged 102-5, compared with the average for the preceding years, 1930, of 113-4, and 119 for 1929. The report continues:
In connection with these indexes it might be mentioned that the present depression has been characterized by a very general movement to retain in so far as possible the usual working force by reducing the hours worked.
The earnings of the persons included in the monthly reports of employment, if available, would, in this way, probably show in many cases a greater decline than the numbers oil the payrolls.
So even accepting these figures, if we take into consideration that many are working on short time, purchasing power as represented by wages has declined much more than would be suggested by the figures given in the indexes.

The preamble of the resolution reads:
And whereas during recent years production has increased enormously.
The mover of the resolution gave ample proof of that recital, and I think it was substantiated by the member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) who preceded me. But perhaps a few further figures along the same lines would not be amiss. In a report made to the international conference of the International Labour Office in May, 1930, there is contained a report from the director, Mr. Albert Thomas, on unemployment and its causes, its extent, and so on. In a lengthy review of the various causes for unemployment, the final point-the ninth point discussed in making out the report was:
9. The disorganization of the labour market caused by the extra-rapid development of labour-saving machinery and of the process of rationalization.
He contended that an inquiry carried out in the United States into the output of workers per working hour showed that this output had increased in 1927 as compared with 1914 as follows:
In slaughterhouses and preserving factories, by 26 per cent.
Cane sugar refining works, by 33 per cent.
Paper factories, by 40 per cent.
Tanneries, by 41 per cent.
Steel works and rolling mills, by 46 per cent.
Cement works, by 54 per cent.
Mills, by 59 per cent.
Petroleum refining works, by 82 per cent.
Blast furnaces, by 103 per cent.
Automobile factories, by 178 per cent.
Tire factories, by 292 per cent.
These figures show a very substantial increase in production per worker in the United States. What is true of that country is largely true of this dominion.
The value of production per individual also increased. In the Monthly Labour Review of the United States for December, 1930, in the period between 1919 and 1929 the value of production per individual worker in the manufacturing industries of the United States increased from 220-5 to 256-2, or 16 per cent. During the same period the index of prices fell by 30 per cent. This means that the actual output really increased by nearly 50 per cent.
Not only has.that increase taken place in industry, but in recent years there has been a similar increase in agriculture. The effects of mechanization were not felt in agriculture . until within comparatively recent years, but now the effect of machinery is apparent. The deputy director of the International Labour

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
Office, Mr. H. B. Butler, reporting on the increased use of agricultural machinery in the United States said:	'
To take one single case: the combine (reaper-thresher) wherever adopted deprives five agricultural workers of employment. And the use of these machines has made immense strides in some countries: in Kansas, for example, there were 14 in 1918, 20,000 in 1928 and 25,000 in 1929, while the figures for Canada are 2 in 1922, 18 in 1925, 4,341 in 1928 and 7,215 in 1929.
A rather peculiar thing in this connection is that while a great number of people were deploring the trend of population from the country to the cities, agricultural production was increasing so fast that it could not be disposed of. In the Canadian Congress Journal for May, 1931, there is an article by Mr. Andrew Stewart, of the University of Manitoba. This article won the prize offered by the Royal Bank of Canada for the best paper on the economy of machine production in agriculture. Mr. Stewart states:
A tractor operator with a five-bottom 14" plough can turn more land in one hour than the same man with a walking plough could cover in a day. Ten days of one man's time are required with a one-horse outfit to cultivate the same acreage that the four-row outfit can cultivate in one day. In 1930, with hand production methods. 32 hours of man labour were required to produce 10 bushels of wheat. In Montana an acre of 'land has been summer-fallowed and a crop of wheat removed the following year with 2-5 hours of man labour. . .
This reduction in labour has resulted in a larger acreage operated per worker. Since 1850 the average acres of improved land per worker in the United States has increased steadily from 30 acres to 49 acres in 1925, and the figures for Canada show that between 1881 and 1891, acres of farm land per worker increased 95 per cent, improved land per worker 105 per cent and crop acres per worker 109 per cent.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
If, as my hon. friend says, the combined reaper harvester enables one man to do the work of five, what reduction would be necessary in the hours of labour of harvesters in order to keep those five men employed in the field?
Mr. MaeINNIS: The hon. member for VVeybum (Mr. Young), representing a country district, perhaps would be better able than I to answer that question. I have not gone into the matter sufficiently to say, but I think I have plainly shown that with present unemployment conditions among the people of Canada, the farmers and the workers, as primary producers, have not received any benefit from the great increase in productive machinery in this country. As a matter of fact we are worse off than we were when production was carried on in a much more primitive way, because at present we are altogether divorced
from a means of livelihood, while in former days we were close to the means of getting a living.
Of course, as the hon. member for Toronto Northwest pointed out, the question of shorter hours is nothing new, but at this time, with unemployment being felt so severely, the matter is being discussed in many places. Last year the question was brought up in the Ontario legislature by Mr. S. C. Tweed, member of the provincial house for North Waterloo. In bringing forward the question Mr. Tweed said:
If we are to depend for a return to prosperity upon an increase in the price of wheat we may have to wait a 'long time. There is no lack of buying power, rather there is concentration of buying power in too few hands.
That is the position we take in bringing forward this resolution. We consider that there is sufficient wealth produced in the country, and all that we need is some means of distributing that wealth. That can be done only through an increase in the purchasing power of -those engaged in industry. In my own province of British Columbia the question was brought forward by Colonel Nelson Spencer, a member of the government party in that province. Mr. Spencer is a lumber operator; he employs a great many men, and he has come to the conclusion that there is no way out of our present difficulties except by Shortening the hours of labour without a corresponding reduction in pay. In that connection I believe he was instrumental in having a resolution passed asking the Dominion government to call a conference of the provincial legislatures in order to discuss this problem.
I wish to point out these facts because undoubtedly if the government speak at all on this matter they will take the stand that they have no jurisdiction over hours of labour. The question of unemployment is so important, and the government of the day must take part in so many phases of provincial legislation and provincial administration which only a few years ago never would have been thought of, that I know the provinces would be pleased and relieved if the federal government would take up this whole question of unemployment purely as a federal measure.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) pointed out that the leader of the Senate has given his benediction to the six-hour day. I know also that Senator A. C. Hardy, speaking before a Rotary club in Brockville in the fall of 1930, said he was convinced of the wisdom of the labour movement in its request for a shorter work day. When the Trades and Labour Congress inter-

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
viewed the government just before the opening of this session the same question was brought up. I should like to read from the memorandum presented by the Trades and Labour Congress to the government, which states:
There has been noticeable, throughout Canada during the past several months a determination on the part of employers to take advantage of the present conditions to reduce wages, notwithstanding there is ample proof that such a policy only results in decreased purchasing power and further aggravation of the unemployment situation.
I may say here that I am sorry the federal government has taken the position adopted by many short-sighted employers of labour, and reduced the salaries paid civil servants. Undoubtedly this will further aggravate the unemployment situation, in that it will reduce purchasing power.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman say in what way this will reduce purchasing power, if that money remains in the country and is not taken up by taxation?

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
It means that the less
purchasing power possessed by workers in industry, the less they can buy. If this money stays in the country that does not mean it is going to be used to purchase commodities. If I have a million dollars I cannot spend all that money in purchasing the things I need, but if I have a thousand dollars I can use that amount and more in the purchase of things I require. When you take ten per cent of that $1,000 you are curtailing my purchasing power, while if you take ten per cent off the million dollars quite possibly it will not affect my purchasing power at all. It may reduce the amount available for savings or for investment in six per cent government bonds, the proceeds of which will be used in meeting the unemployment situation.
The memorandum goes on to say:
We believe that by a liberal administration of the Fair Wages Act the government could assist materially to offset this by maintaining wage rates on works undertaken or assisted by the government, even though employers may in some districts have succeeded, temporarily, in reducing wages below what would be considered in ordinary times as "fair and reasonable."
The existing fair wages policy up to the time of enactment of the Fair Wages Act had been based on the existing conditions in respect to hours of labour which often resulted in unreasonably long work days. We believe that present conditions warrant a policy of still further reduction of hours in order to give a larger number of workers opportunity for employment. We would therefore urge the government both in respect to contracts coming within the scope of the fair wage policy and its own works, to,

wherever practical, put into effect the six hour day and five day week and by this means give a lead to private industry in a matter that cannot help but reflect itself in a reduction of the number of unemployed workers. In doing this, however, due consideration should be given to the payment of wages high enough to maintain established standards of living, as otherwise no real relief would result. Wage reductions have not been accompanied by any reduction in interest rates on loans, but on the contrary there has been a tendency to pay higher interest rates presumably to ensure the successful flotation of government bonds. This again we believe leads to a decrease in the amount of money available for purchases and a reduction of a demand for goods on the part of the masses.
In connection with their request for an extension of the six-hour day, they also made a further case for the ratification of the eight-hour day convention, pointing out that the government in its own employ at the present time has men working as many as twelve hours a day. I refeT to guards in penitentiaries where men are still working twelve hours a day, despite the fact that the government is paying direct relief to able-bodied men who would be able to do this work.
I have two more quotations to make. In this connection I think it is well to observe that the seriousness of the unemployment situation is making it possible to discuss this question in a better spirit than was possible some years ago. It is not so very long ago since, if you mentioned the matter of unemployment, you were reminded that people who were unemployed were unemployed because of their own shortcomings. To-day no one makes that statement. I noticed, in a report which appeared in the Toronto Globe, a speech made in Windsor, Ontario, by the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) on Oetdber 16, 1931. I do not know at the moment what particular organization he was addressing, but I would give this brief quotation from (his remarks. He said:
We are spending $50,000,000 this year to give temporary relief to the families affected by the depression.
That is quite an item for a government to be spending-a government that was going to deal with the unemployment situation without having recourse to doles. The minister continued:
We cannot continue to spend this amount every year for this purpose. There must be an end to the peak of prosperity and the depth of depression.
And now comes a very important point which the minister made:
The human element is thrown out when the factories close down. This has been going on

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Vallance
for years. Industrial leaders, instead of inventing new machinery that means less work for the workmen, should evolve and devise some social machine that will forever put an end to such situations as now confront this country.
The Minister of Railways puts his finger on the vital point in capitalistic production when he states that the human element, that is, the workers in industry, are thrown out when the factories close down. The factories close down when profit cannot be made from operating them, for profit is the motive underlying production. He says that industrial leaders, instead of inventing new machinery that means less work for the workmen, should evolve some social machine that will forever put an end to such situations as now confront this country. But may I point out that industrial leaders are not interested in the human factor in industry; they are interested only in profits, and they install machinery in factories, not to ease the burdens on the backs of workers but to increase their own profits. How, therefore, can the minister expect such men to use their time in trying to evolve and devise some social machine that will forever put an end to such situations as now confront the country? If such a scheme is evolved that scheme will have to be put into effect, even, in my opinion, against the opposition of such leaders of industry, because it will take away from them their prerogative of making a profit out of the needs of the workers of the country. I submit that the present government should take the case up now, for if they do not do so some other government will have to do it later on.
Now I wish to quote an item from an address given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). He was speaking to The Advertising and Sales Roundtable in the convention hall of the Royal York Hotel on October 28, 1931, and in the course of his remarks he said:
We are unworthy of our marvellous heritage if we cannot take it and transmute it into something of which we can be increasingly proud.
We certainly cannot be increasingly proud of what we have to-day.
If we have learned the lessons of the past few years, and if we can bring distribution into equitable alignment with the growth of our production, then 1932 may well be the opening year in the new era of Canadian contact with the economic world.
This is rather a strange statement coming from a gentleman who in May last, when the motion which was passed in this house a few days ago was being discussed, said that there was nothing particularly wrong in the alignment between distribution and production. Possibly we should be glad that what we
have been saying here, along, of course, with economic conditions, is having some effect on the point of view of members of the government.
I do not think I need say anything further on this subject, but I hope that some member of the government will discuss the question. The question of unemployment is becoming increasingly serious and some steps should be taken to deal with it. I am just as firmly convinced as the Minister of Railways that this country cannot go on spending money year after year in trying to promote public works and in giving doles and direct relief to unemployed people, thereby piling up a debt, the carrying charges of which must be met. Something must be done. The wealth of the country must in some way be produced and distributed to those who need it, and in my opinion, under present conditions, there is only one way of doing this and that is by increasing the purchasing power of the workers in industry. That can be done, if both the product of industry and its production are fairly shared. I trust that the government will receive this resolution favourably and that we shall hear from them to that effect.

I merely wrote down the statement of the hon. member and if he says he did not make it, the statement that he makes now comes finally to the same thing. In my opinion the trouble with capital is that the capitalists are demanding too much of the benefit that has been derived from the machine age. There are only four sources of wealth in any country:	the four natural resources,
namely, the forests, fisheries, agriculture, and mines. Without the application of labour those things are of no value, but labour to-day does not receive back its share of the cost of the fabrication and we find stacked up in the shelves what we propose to call too great overproduction. The trouble is that labour has not been getting that amount which will enable labour to buy back that which it has created. The last speaker has pointed out that under the profit system you can extract profit from only one source, and that is from the production of the goods, a certain percentage of the goods. According to the percentage that capital demands as a profit, just so long will it take to pile those goods up because of labour's inability to buy back that which it has created.
Coming from the prairies as I do, farming as I do, using all the modern machinery as I do, I should like to point out that in spite of the labour reductions that I can show, in the turnover of my business every year, to me, to the labourer still on that farm-talking of myself-I own no more at the end of the year than I did when we used the sickle and the walking plough. Why? Because labour and capital-I am talking of industrialists now- are demanding from me more than I am able to pay. Until that condition is rectified, how can we take two men to produce forty cent wheat where one is doing it to-day, and at the same time say that you can maintain the standard of living to those two? It cannot be done. I have laboured and I can tell labour this, that until the primary producer finds himself in a position to buy those goods which the industrialists create, we shall find ourselves always in the same situation.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN HOURS OF LABOUR TO PROVIDE WORK FOR UNEMPLOYED AND INCREASE PURCHASING POWER
speechtext:
Inasmuch as this question of unemployment is one of great national importance I should like the house to get a clearer understanding of just what the resolution means. I do not rise to give that explanation myself because I am not clear on the point, but we ought to understand what it means before we vote upon it. I think the mover of the resolution (Mr. Heaps) has not taken the house entirely into his confidence in his exposition of the resolution.
Everyone will agree with the first statement of the resolution, that there are great numbers of our citizens at present unemployed and that through their unemployment their very existence is made precarious. We will also agree with the further statement that during recent years production has increased enormously. I was reading only this afternoon in the report of the Macmillan committee that production throughout the entire world had increased since 1913 by 25 per cent. So there cannot be much doubt about that. The next statement in the resolution is this:
Whereas real wages have not increased in proportion and thus consumption has not kept pace with production.
Of course, it is simply another truth to say that consumption has not kept pace with production, for the reason that wages have not increased in proportion with the increase in production.
Now I come to the declaratory part of the resolution:
Be it resolved: That, in the opinion of this house, in order to absorb the unemployed into industry, thus eliminating the enormous waste of enforced idleness, the hours of labour be materially reduced and the purchasing power of the masses increased, and further to this end that the government be requested to submit the necessary measures to the house.
Let us look at what that means. If it merely means what has been the policy of the organized Labour movement of Canada for many years, in respect to wages, then it means nothing. That policy has been and is that the wages of labourers can be and should be increased, in the vain hope that in doing so the standard of living and purchasing power will be increased. But here is the problem:	We are operating under a profit
system, and under a profit system an increase of wages must necessarily mean a corresponding increase in the price of commodities in the production of which wages are paid; so that ultimately an increase in wages must be balanced by an increase in prices, except in the case of overhead savings through improved organization or improved machinery, with such savings going to wages instead of to cheaper goods. To ask for wage increases or hour reduction under a profit system is to work around in a circle. That has been the weakness of the policy of labour ever since I knew anything about it. Even strikes never got labour anywhere, because it was not possible to have a real increase in wages under a profit system since wage increases were invariably offset by an increase in the price of commodities.
If it means that there must be a reduction of the hours of labour and an increase in pay under the present profit system, then it is impossible. If then the resolution means anything it means that we are asked to introduce a new system. That is what the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) must have in mind, and if so he is not following his usual frank way of dealing with things if he does not say so. He asks the house to introduce legislation as quickly as possible to implement this resolution. I would like to know what that means. Is it that the government should introduce by legislation a new economic system into Canada? That means, if it means anything, that the government must first nationalize the industrial system in

Unemployment Relie]-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
this country. If the resolution means that, I will vote for it because I have always stood for that; I like it. If it does not mean that, it does not mean anything at all, and I would not be bothered voting for it. I would like somebody to explain just exactly what this resolution means. If it stands for a new system, which if it means anything it must mean, I would like to vote for it. If it stands for the old impossible system of increasing wages and shortening hours and increasing prices, the thing is ridiculous. Now will somebody explain?

That, in the opinion of this house, in order to absorb the unemployed into industry, thus eliminating the enormous waste of enforced idleness, the hours of labour be materially reduced and the purchasing power of the masses increased.

It is the habit for the official members of the Labour party to move resolutions of this kind without ever looking at the question of jurisdiction. For the moment I am content to admit the force of my hon. friend's logic. He has not shown any real iogic, however, but only word logic.
What about our wheat? We have disposed of more of our wheat abroad than we did last year-far more. We have not lost our markets, and are in a fair way to gain others.
I should like to say to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg that I represent a large number of labour people, and if he hopes to continue to represent and to serve labour^ in this house he should introduce a resolution within our jurisdiction, and one whereby we could accomplish something of a practical nature. We do not want mere propaganda, but something which, in the interests of labour and the people of Canada generally, will help us to solve this problem.
I consider that the resolution is nothing more than mere verbiage. I therefore oppose it. Before taking my seat however I should like to say that I believe my hon. friends from Winnipeg North and Vancouver South are actuated by high and altruistic motives. But when we try to foist upon our industrial system an abstract scheme such as the one now before us we are not trying to solve the problems of Canada but are introducing merely a resolution which means nothing, will get us nowhere and, in my humble opinion, will work to the detriment of Canada.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I oppose this resolution.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, on one occasion when
a barrister was appealing before an appellate court from a judgment issued by a lower court
he said to the appellate judges, "I am appealing from the judgment of Mr. Justice So-and-So." Then the judges asked him, "Have you any other reason for appealing from this judgment?" The idea contained in the resolution is one brought in from the United States, and that is one of the reasons I am not prepared to accept it. There are other reasons however which I shall undertake to outline. If we reduce the number of working hours we will not solve the problem of unemployment but will only displace it.
I have only one further remark to make, namely, that since the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) declared that if he came into power he would end unemployment, I am very much surprised that no effective steps have been taken in that direction. At the special session the first action to relieve unemployment was to apply a plaster of $20,000,000, and following that to increase the tariff. Was that good or was it bad? Events have proved the lack of wisdom in these actions. During the war many people were wounded, but the same cure was not applied to all. Different diseases require different cures, and my suggestion would be that before we discuss further the great and difficult problem of unemployment an inventory be made of all our unemployed, setting out their previous occupations, reasons for unemployment and the concerns for whom they were working before they became unemployed. To my mind those facts should be known before any attempt is made to cure the evil. Undoubtedly such a survey would cost money, but having been done we would know, once and for all, exactly where we stand. I remember having read last year statements from the then Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) to the effect that within a few months we would hear no more about unemployment, that everyone would have work to do and would be employed at some work for which he was fitted. The statistics we have received are to the effect that while the minister was making such statements the figures from his own department told a different story. For that reason I suggest to the Prime Minister- who, I am happy to say, is with us for another few seconds-and to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), to consider my suggestion and make an inventory of the unemployed. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will engage the attention of the house only a few moments with respect to this resolution. I think it obvious that both inside and outside this chamber there are two distinct schools of thought with respect to labour. The followers of one school are content to toil and by their thrift to advance themselves, while those of the other school are probably drifting the opposite way. There is not any doubt in my mind that every member of this house is anxious to seek some means whereby those who depend upon their livelihood in industry, and consequently upon the activities of those who employ them, shall be employed and remunerated at such a rate that they will be able to take their place in the life of their country, support their families, and carrying on as good citizens, in the aggregate help to build up a strong and great nation. No one will deny that that is the right of every Canadian citizen. I am not at all in agreement with those who make the statement that leaders of industry direct their attention wholly to profits and do not concern themselves with the interests of their employees. During my lifetime I have been associated with leaders of industry, although I must confess that I have never reaped the fabulous rewards from that contact that I have heard referred to in this house. In fact, in the short time that I have been a member, I have heard more of the huge profits that leaders of industry make than I ever learned of when I was outside and had some contact with those same men. Undoubtedly there is truth in what those who claim to be the exponents of labour say, that from time to time as depression falls upon us, and even in prosperous times, a section of our workingmen do not receive adequate remuneration for their labour.
So far as the resolution is concerned, I am persuaded that this parliament can do but little to carry into effect what it proposes.
I am sure hon. members realize that if we attempted to carry out what is proposed we would be immediately confronted with pro-

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gordon
tests on the part of the provinces that we were infringing their rights, because while we are a federal union we are not a legislative union, and the provinces jealously guard the rights that were conferred upon them at confederation. It is quite true that the Treaty of Versailles did in terms suggest that all the nations of the world should get together in some way-it was not stated specifically how they should do it-and pass laws that would destroy the possibility of war and industrial conflict. In fact, it seemed to be the expectation that almost every ill that besets the human race would be entirely remedied by the passage of resolutions. Amongst others, this very subject was dealt with in that treaty. It has been discussed in this house before, and I presume it will be discussed again. In my view the federal parliament has not within its legislative power the right to do what the resolution proposes. True it is that by conference with the provinces and by a closer understanding between industry and labour great strides have been made in improving industrial conditions, and probably still greater strides will be made in the future. But when any hon. member stands up in this house and suggests that we can put the farmer on a five hour day, then I must confidently assert that he does not know very much about farming. Such a proposal is utterly impossible and cannot be worked out. With respect to the discussions that have taken place as to the reduction of the hours of labour, no one has suggested to what point they shall be reduced, or whether all industries shall be treated alike. On the other hand no one has suggested any solution to the problem of what to do with the resultant increase in the products of industry. Who is to buy them if prices go up? It seems to me that in past years I have heard the subject matter of this resolution discussed many times by economists, and I note that they found the same trouble in arriving at a solution that I have always found-the question whether it was going to be of any material help to the people concerned.
Just in passing let me say this: I was impressed by the suggestion made by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt). If it means anything, this resolution is very comprehensive in its terms. It covers more than Canada; it is universal in its application if it can be applied at all, and I am at an utter loss to know what measures this house could bring down that would be effective. I think perhaps we have learned something from the discussion that has taken place, but I know
of no measure that could be introduced in this house that would bring to fruition the idea contained in the resolution. The one burden, if you call it that, which is cast upon us at all times, and I think particularly at times like these, is to take care of the people within our boundaries and to see that their future is not imperilled by any conscious act of any government which is in power in this country. I wonder at times, however, if those who take the part of labour stop when their advocacy ceases, or if their concrete actions reflect the same ardour. In the last hour or two I have surveyed the records 'of the number of people brought into this country prior to that fateful July 28, 1930, in order to see to what extent those who take the part of labour really had labour at heart in the two or three years prior to that date. I find that one very ardent advocate of labour in this house, through his applications for permits for the admission of people into Canada, brought into this country 345 people, all of whom entered into some form of industry although each was supposed to take up agriculture. If every member and every defeated candidate had availed himself of a similar privilege our labour problem in this country would have been increased by 169.050 people. That is just a passing observation, but I think those who advocate the position of labour should be extremely careful to see that their interest does not cease with a verbal advocacy.
With respect to the resolution itself, in my view-and I think it is shared by those who have given this subject any considerable thought-this House of Commons has not the legislative power to bring in a measure that would carry into effect what is suggested in the resolution, and I seriously doubt if any committee of this house or any committee of economists could sit about a table and devise a scheme that would apply to all the different forms of industry and agriculture, giving effect to the idea contained in this resolution. I think at this time the house would be well advised to let the resolution drop, with the discussion that has taken place so far in connection with it.
