I withdraw the imputation, Mr. Speaker. Now, I have in my hand the Canadian Unionist of October 1931, which gives the attitude of the government. My speech is reported in full, and the conclusion of the report is this:
Although Mr. Heenan's motion had the support of all parties, it was deliberately talked out by J. H. Stitt, the Conservative member for Selkirk, self-styled friend of the workers.
So that we 'have this resolution before the house again because of the fact that the 'hon. member did talk out the previous one, whether or not 'he intended to.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said over and over again, especially during the election time, that if the federal government did its duty no man or woman who was willing to work should do without work. The Afinister of Labour now stands in his place, after the government has failed to end unemployment, and says that he doubts very much whether this house can do anything in the matter as regards providing measures to relieve unemployment, or providing for shorter hours, or assimilating workers in industry. If I remember rightly, the present Prime Minister once said that we had .the power; he said that if this parliament wished to insert a provision in our tariff legislation to provide for shorter hours or for any other condition with regard to workers, it had the power to do so. It appears, therefore, that we have now what is known as governmental solidarity, the present Prime Minister taking the view that we have the power and the Minister of
Labour declaring that he does not see anything within the four walls Of parliament that could give us that power.
The Minister of Labour also made certain references to the farming community. If I remember rightly, he said: Show me Where a shorter working day could be applied to agriculture. Well, I know that the present Minister of Labour has not been in his position very long and that is the excuse I would make for him; because he will find there is no labour delegation or labour platform that has ever suggested that a shorter working day should 'apply to agriculture. Indeed, the treaty of Versailles and the conventions arising out of it all exempted the agriculturists from the eight-hour day, so that there is no necessity for bringing up that bogey with respect to the eight-hour or the shorter working day as applied to agriculture.
The Alinister of Labour concluded his observations by saying that he was at a loss to know what measures could be taken to reduce the hours of labour, which is really what the resolution calls for. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), when he was leader of the opposition, announced a policy, as I stated before, that we could take measures by way of providing in the tariff legislation that any industry that secured the protection afforded by such legislation should manifest to the government or some commission that it was maintaining the eight-hour day, or the six-hour day or any hour day that the government might wish to impose. They could do all that is possible to stop the reduction in wages that is taking place all over Canada, but so far there is in this country, generally speaking, a reduction in wages ranging anywhere from ten to twenty-five per cent, and the government, so far as I am aware, have not taken any measures whatever to stop or to try to stop it. It is true some members of the cabinet have asked publicly that employers should keep on as many employees as possible during this period of depression and that they should not take advantage of the depressed times to reduce wages; but notwithstanding that, reductions in wages have taken place all over Canada just the same. Indeed, the government itself is leading the way by dismissing many men from the public service, and by making a reduction in wages.
Our railroad men, who are just now suffering a reduction of ten per cent, had, when the Conservatives were in power in 1921, to take a reduction to the extent of 12 1-2 per cent in wages, or about $45,000,000 a year. That is what they contributed to the prosperity of the country. It is true that they got back

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heenan
upwards of six per cent of that between 1927 and 1930, but now they are again faced with the ten per cent reduction in wages, and I ask the Minister of Labour or any other member of the government: what have they _ done to prevent that reduction in wages? The railroads of Canada are under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, and I have yet to hear of or see one iota of action the government have taken to stop that reduction in wages. Indeed, they have accepted the report of a board of conciliation and investigation which practically discards the announced policy and principle of the federal government with respect to wages as applied to railroad men. I have under my hand a copy of an order in council dated 16th July, 1918. I do not want to read it all because it is a very lengthy document, but in it there is this principle announced:
And it further appears that the railroad companies are of the view that the wages paid railway employees in Canada ought to be the same as that adopted in corresponding territories in the United States, as the class of work is the same in both countries.
That is an announced principle which was adopted by the governor general in council. This year the government appoints a board of conciliation and investigation and we have this reference:
As regards the employees' second point, we feel that railway basic wage rates in Canada must be based on conditions in Canada and not in the United States. We feel that the capacity to earn revenue must be an important element in the payment of wages, and in the United States railway earning conditions are substantially different from those of Canadian railways.
I have yet to hear some protest from either the Minister of Labour or any other member of the government with respect to that recommendation of the board of conciliation which discards the principle that they themselves enunciated in 1918. The Canadian railroad men are loyal to this country. As I said, they contributed $45,000,000 annually out of their wages by taking the reduction in 1921. They have accepted the reduction this year because of their loyalty to the country, because they have heard politicians tell them from every platform and in the House of Commons that prosperity is just around the corner and they are loath to be the ones that would attempt to put a drag on that prosperity from coming around that corner.
But, as I said, the government of Canada has jurisdiction over the railways. They could and the railway companies could have found on the railways many other avenues where they could have saved, but they started to reduce wages. If you read the newspapers of

this country you will find that very few of the writers have much knowledge with respect to the earnings of railroad men or the conditions of their employment. They take one or two or a dozen of the highest paid men on the highest paid runs and they put down their earnings as an average for the railroad men. They forget there are between 25,000 and 30,000 railroad men who have worked ten and twenty years, many of whom work only three or at most four months a year, and who are laid off because of seasonal traffic. They also forget at the present time there is upwards of $200,000,000 worth of rolling stock that is tied up on the side tracks, not used, that has to be paid for with interest and that is charged up to the railroad companies, and yet the railroad men's wages are the first to be attacked. They forget the millions of dollars tied up in the terminals, in the shops, in equipment of all kinds, that have been paid for with interest out of the revenues of the railroad companies, and that is lying idle, and the only thing it seems that they can save on, is the railroad men's wages.
I want to point this out very clearly, because the board has taken the position that a railroad man's wages in Canada ought not to be on a par with those that are earned in the United States. The railroad men of this country are not only loyal but efficient. We have to compare the operation of our Canadian railroads with the operation of those of the United States, because they are the only ones that are comparable, the railroads of Canada and the United States being equipped to haul long trains long distances, whereas the European railroads are equipped to haul short trains short distances. It is on record to-day that the railway men of Canada handle about twelve thousand tons of freight per man per mile more than do the railroad men in the United States. Yet we have a board appointed by the government bringing in a recommendation that, notwithstanding this display of efficiency and loyalty, the wages of the railroad men of Canada are not entitled to be put on the same basis as those of the railroad men of the United States.
There is no necessity to read this resolution again. It simply asks the government to submit the necessary measures to the house. The Minister of Labour says that he does not agree with the resolution. I hope he does not speak for the whole government. I hope we are not going to have government solidarity on this occasion, because there are many things that could be done. The government has power to bring in measures reducing the hours of work in industry under its tariff

legislation. They have power to initiate a program of public works to be gone on with to provide work for the unemployed. They have power to go on with the trans-Canada highway, which they promised the electors of this country. They have many opportunities. Having failed in their promise to end unemployment, having failed to live up to the principle which they enunciated that if the government of Canada did its duty every man and woman in this country willing to work would have the opportunity to work; having failed miserably in all these things we have the spectacle of the Minister of Labour standing in his place to-day-not speaking for the government-and saying: I am at a loss to know what we can do in the matter.

While I am in sympathy with labour in desiring to see this unemployment problem solved so that they can get more pay and less work, I have very little sympathy with this government which made such rash preelection promises, for no other purpose, apparently, than to obtain office; because they must have known that they could not do the

He says that he has listened to several economists speaking on it and that apparently the economists, one and all, were unable to lay their finger on the solution of the problem of unemployment. speechtext:
My hon. friends laugh.
I will read something to them and probably they will laugh on the other side of their faces. This is from a bulletin published by the Chase National bank of the city of New York. It is an article on the tariff and the world depression by Mr. Benjamin M. Anderson, economist of that bank. He says:
We are in the midst of a severe business depression which is world wide. The most serious obstacle in the way of early recovery is the state of our foreign trade. The most serious obstacle in the way of the revival of our foreign trade is our high protective tariffs, the quickest way to get out of the existing depression is to reduce our tariffs so that our foreign customers may sell more goods here and get more dollars with which to pay interest upon their debts to us and with which to buy our goods. If we do not buy we cannot sell. If we do not buy enough we cannot sell enough.
I do not hear my hon. friends laughing now. Then listen to this:
Bankers and economists have been telling the country this ever since the world war, but the country has been slow in learning the lesson.
That lesson is being brought home to us to-day, and if we wish to cure unemployment and get out of the depression in which we find ourselves to-day there is only one way. If we want to sell more we must buy more. The Prime Minister said the other day that the only way to get a favourable balance of trade was to cut down our imports. Why, Mr. Speaker, any child knows that there is another way. Why not increase our exports? There are two ways of doing it. You can get a favourable balance of trade by increasing exports just as well as by cutting down our imports and throttling business. If

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Donnelly
we had more exports we would find our markets increasing all over the world and our labourers would be employed in our factories and in our means of transportation.
We hear a lot about the new factories that are coming to this country and of the improvement that has taken place under the higher tariff, but we had the spectacle of the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) rising in the house this afternoon and saying: In my constituency it is not a case of a shorter day or a shorter week; it is a case of no work. Yet we are being told that the factories in the industrial centres are working overtime on account of this great tariff. When I listened to the speech of the Prime Minister before the last election I thought there was going to be no trouble whatever. He said that the country was in a terrible condition, that it was very sick. He reminded me of a physician who goes to see a patient suffering from fever, accompanied by a severe headache. He says to his patient: I will give you this pill for your headache and this boittle of medicine to cure your permanent disease. In the same way the Prime Minister in September 1630 called a special session. He was the great physician who was going to cure unemployment. He said to his patient: I am going to give you this temporary relief, this small pill of $20,000,000 which will ease your unemployment for a while, and then here is a bottle of dope which is the great cure that is going to make you young and well. Take that and everything will be all right again. This bottle of dope is labelled "higher tariffs." We have been taking the medicine steadily; we had more of it last session, and the public is still asking for more. WTe are still getting bigger and bigger doses of that permanent cure, and yet the patient is getting sicker and sicker every day, until at last the Prime Minister himself has thrown up his hands and has had to admit, as he did when speaking to a meeting of one of the United Churches lately: Nothing but the grace of God, he said, can save this country. He admits he is wrong. He said that he would cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. Well, he is perishing in the attempt. He is failing to cure unemployment. I say we are not going to have better times or any improvement in this country until we increase our export markets. When we increase our exports we will begin to buy more, and when we begin to buy more we will sell more. At a time when we begin to buy and sell more and begin to trade more with our neighbouring countries, conditions will improve. The Liberal

policy as enunciated by Hon. Charles Dunning indicated that we were willing to trade with those who would trade with us; that is the Liberal policy, and that is the policy to which we are pledged to-day.

My hon. friend may consult the Canada Year Book to get that information; I am sorry I have not the information under my band. I wish to tell him bowever that between the years 1921 and 1929 there was an increase of about 60 per cent, and I will add that Canada never was more prosperous than during those years. I will say more than that; I will tell my hon. friend that we took power at a time of depression and brought conditions back to prosperity.
Let us survey the history of Canada for the last thirty-five years; for the benefit of my hon. friend I should be pleased to trace it. Back in the year 1895 we were suffering from a depression, and at that time we had a Conservative government. In 1896 the Liberal party came into power, and through Sir Wilfrid Laurier a Liberal policy was put into effect whereby we showed a willingness to trade with those who would trade with us. We put into effect a British preferential tariff; we lowered the duty; and prosperity in Canada extended to the year 1911. At that time we tried to put into effect the very same policy that the Liberal party has always preached, to trade -with those who trade with us. We were willing to put through a measure of reciprocity to enable freeT trade with the United States. Out in the west however a lack of patriotism was preached and as a result we were defeated. No greater calamity ever overtook this country than the rejection of reciprocity. The people realize that to-day, and our agriculturists sineeTely believe it. From the years 1911 to 1914 Canada went through another period of depression, and conditions became worse and worse until war broke out. When the weu- was over and the Conservative party took over the reins of power we entered another period of depression which became worse and worse until the Liberal party again took office in 1921. They proceeded to put into effect the very same policy they had always believed in, that of trading with those who would trade with us. Conditions became better and better from year to year until the last election, when our Conservative friends obtained a majority, and as a result trade has been restricted and we

are again in a period of depression. If my hon. friends will look back over the past tihirty-five years they will find that not once has there been prosperity during the regime of a Conservative government. If any of my hon. friends dispute that fact I challenge them to tell me the years, during the last thirty-five years, when during the time of a Conservative government we have had prosperity.
May I say to my hon. friend who interrupted that he will have the opportunity to speak when I have resumed my seat, and I ask him to tell me the years when we have had prosperity. Any prosperity Canada has enjoyed has -been under a Liberal government, and any prosperity we will ever have will be under a Liberal government. The economics of my hon. friends opposite are altogether wrong; their principles are wrong. They cannot restrict trade and have prosperity.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to have an improvement in this unfortunate condition of unemployment there is only one way to do it, namely to cut down our tariff wall and trade with those who will trade with us. If we do that we will give employment to our people and return the country to that state of prosperity it enjoyed before the last election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word concerning this very important resolution. Whether we agree with the wording of the resolution or the theory advocated by its mover (Mr. Heaps) we must admit that the subject matter is of great importance. What could be more important at this time than the question of employment for the masses of our people? In my opinion parliament would be well advised to give .more heed to and spend more time in discussing this subject.
One point has not been 'brought out in the various arguments advanced; I refer to the increasing numbers of our young men and women who upon reaching manhood and womanhood can find no useful employment, be 'they ever so eager to procure it. I have talked with many men and women who are almost distracted with the grave problem of unemployment which is affecting their grown up sons and daughters who find they have nothing to do and have to remain at home in idleness. I realize there are some hon. members in this house who believe that if we only wait a little while everything will turn out all right and matters will be adjusted. Perhaps they believe the tariff will solve our unemployment problem, if we but
have the patience to wait. I am glad to say that I for one do not share those views; for I am of opinion that with our modern labour saving machinery, industry, as we know it, will never again be able to absorb and give employment to the millions of able-bodied men and women throughout the world who desire it. I believe that should be borne in mind by the heads of governments and should be the basis from which to begin in an endeavour to find employment for those who must have it.
I am not sure whether or not the proposed resolution, if put into practice, would solve the difficulty, because as yet no one has been able to determine either by mathematics or by statistics just how many hours workers would have to be employed so that everyone might be engaged. I am firmly convinced however that if no attempt is made to solve the difficulty it will not solve itself, and I am wondering how much worse conditions have to become in Canada before some action, different from that which has been taken, will be taken to cope with the problem of unemployment. Conditions would be much better in my opinion if fewer hours of labour were necessary, coupled with the control of wealth, which is now in the hands of only a few. In that way employment would be given to greater numbers. If conditions do not improve the lesser number of our people engaged in occupations and receiving wages will be taxed to support the great numbers who, through no fault of their own, cannot procure suitable or, in fact, any employment and are forced to partake of charity. The cry of the masses must be heard, and cannot much longer be ignored.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considering this question of unemployment I think we would do well to carry our minds back to those primitive times when each family was a selLcontained economic unit, cultivated a small piece of ground with implements of their own faishioning, built their own houses out of such material as could be readily found; when the furniture was made from blocks of wood chopped off the end of a log, when clothing was made from wool sheared from their own sheep, spun and woven mto cloth, and fashioned into garments by the women of the household, and when everything was produced in the home. In those days there was no unemployment; there was plenty of work for everybody. If nature was kind and gave a fruitful harvest there was plenty to eat and plenty to wear. If nature was unkind and the crops in any particular

* Unemployment Relief-Mr. Young
locality failed, starvation stared them in the face; for there were no facilities to bring goods from a distance. I say there was no unemployment at that time; everybody had to work hard, long hours for a very meagre subsistence.
Compare the standard of living of an ordinary citizen in those days with the standard of living of an ordinary citizen to-day. Then he lived in a hovel with probably a thatched roof and a mud floor, with hardly any window, perhaps a sheepskin nailed over a hole in the wall, and a blanket for a door. He had no reading matter, no opportunities for education, no fine raiment, no musical instruments -something that we to-day consider necessary for a civilized being to enjoy life. Go into the home of an ordinary workingman to-day and you will find that it is a palace compared with what his predecessor lived in; you will find he has light, books to read, a telephone,
[DOT] a piano, a radio, opportunities for education- many things that even the richest could not enjoy in those days.
I ask you, what has brought about this change in the condition of the workingman? It resulted from the division of labour from improved methods of production. It was found that a man making his own tools, cultivating his own farm, shoeing his own horse, building his own house, making his own furniture, could not do much of anything in a given time. It was found that by a division of labour, by some men confining their attention to the production of those things which they could produce to the best advantage, while others confined their attention to the production of other things in which they excelled, it was passible to increase the total production of the human race manyfold. That process continued and was accelerated from time to time, until to-day men specialize in one branch of any particular industry. This has brought about a vast increase in the production of all kinds of wealth-much more wealth of every kind is now available for the consumption of the human race. The result is a much higher standard of living, and the world is able to sustain many times the population she could sustain in those days, and many times what she could sustain to-day were it not for these modern labour-saving devices.
I do not agree with those who say there is overproduction of wealth to-day; there is no overproduction of wealth. I do not agree with those who say we have solved the problem of production; we have not. We have not come anywhere near solving the problem of producing all the goods that the world can consume. Our capacity to consume food

is limited by the capacity of our stomachs; but our capacity to consume other commodities is unlimited. Overproduction of all goods? A thousand million people in the world to-day are not getting enough to eat. If you could add one slice of bread at each meal for those people it would require an additional two thousand million bushels of wheat a year. Can there be any overproduction of wheat while a condition like that exists? Overproduction of clothing? There are ten million people in Canada, and nine million, nine hundred thousand of them would do well to have more clothes. The same is true of our houses, our furniture, everything. There is no overproduction of wealth in the world to-day, and any scheme that aims to curtail the production of wealth will aggravate unemployment and lower the standard of living.
Now, we have seen that this division of labour and improvement in methods of production by improved machinery and otherwise has made it possible to produce many times more wealth than before. But that presupposes that those who produce one kind of wealth must be in a position to exchange it with those who produce another kind of wealth. Bring about these conditions where those who produce a surplus of wealth can exchange their surplus with those who produce a surplus of other wealth, and you have solved the problem of unemployment. Why is it, then, that we have unemployment? Because something stops us from exchanging the goods which we produce in abundance for the goods that we require and that other people produce in abundance. We in Canada can produce the basic products in abundance-lumber, pulpwood, newsprint, fish, minerals, wheat and so on; other countries can produce other things in abundance; but so long as governments interfere and say, "We will not allow you to exchange the things that you have to sell for the things that other people have to sell," just so long will there be unemployment.

Yes, tariffs. I thank my
hon. friend for the suggestion. Tariffs, I say, are the main cause of all our troubles. Let me give you an illustration. A certain farmer in a dried-out district of Saskatchewan last year planted a field of potatoes in the bed of a lake that had gone dry; he harvested a good crop; nobody else in the neighbourhood had any potatoes; that farmer has more potatoes than he can use, he has potatoes to sell, but he cannot sell a bushel of them.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps
Why? Overproduction of potatoes? No, there is an actual scarcity of potatoes in that district. Why cannot he sell them? Because his neighbours have nothing to give him in exchange. Do you expect a man who produces one thing to give it away to somebody else who has nothing to give him in return? No. Those who produce one commodity must be in a position to exchange with those who produce something else.
We in Canada produce certain things; other people in other countries produce other things. The unemployed in Canada are not in a position to give us anything for the goods that the employed people are producing. If those who are producing in Canada were permitted to exchange their products for the products of the people of other countries, they would be able to purchase more goods in Canada, they wTould be able to enlarge their operations, they would be able to employ more men, and unemployment would disappear. Any attempt to remedy unemployment by decreasing the amount of wealth produced would have the very opposite effect; but every step taken to remove the trade barriers which prevent those who have wealth from exchanging it for other forms of wealth that others have to sell is a step toward the removal of unemployment. Until these barriers are done away with, we will have unemployment, and we will have it in worse form as time goes on.

I
was very glad to observe that those who have participated in this debate have expressed so much sympathy with the working people. We are thankful for those expressions, but we should like something more definite and concrete to help the unemployed-something more than sympathy. With the argument of the last speaker (Mr. Young) I do not altogether agree. I am of the opinion that if the whole world at the present time went entirely on a free trade basis there still would be unemployment. In a very limited time we could produce more than enough to satisfy all our requirements, and I think on
that basis four hours of work a day would be more than sufficient to satisfy human requirements, including those of the farmers!

I might as well ask my hon. friend what evidence he has that everyone would be happy if the world went on a free trade basis. I think the tremendous increase in production, our modern methods and machine equipment which is displacing labour, are sufficient proofs of the statement I am making to the house.
So the problem is not one of production or of exchange; it is a problem of distribution. If a man is working for wages and is getting only one-fifth or one-quarter of what he produces, it would be the same if he were living under protection or under free trade, and until we can break down that spread between what a man receives in wages and the value of what he produces, in my opinion, there is no hope of solving the problem of unemployment.
Something has been said during the course of this debate with regard to jurisdiction. I recognize the limitations imposed on this parliament; I recognize the difficulties connected with jurisdiction with which we are confronted, but if we are always to set up that question of jurisdiction I am afraid it will be very difficult for us to make much progress in this country. I remember that a few years ago, when the question of old age pensions was raised in the house, we were met with the plea of lack of jurisdiction, but when parliament determined to provide the aged people of this country with old age pensions, ways and means were found to overcome that difficulty. Just as we overcame the question of jurisdiction in regard to old age pensions, so I am satisfied we could overcome the difficulty of jurisdiction which faces us in connection with this problem, once the house is determined to do so.
Credit has been taken for what has been done by the government in order to assist the unemployment situation. I wish to say here that I greatly appreciate what has been done by the government during the past twelve or eighteen months in helping the municipalities and the provinces to deal with this unemployment problem, but when I make that statement that is as far as I can go. What they are doing is in no way a solution of the problem; it deals in no fundamental way with this great question. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that the continual giving of these doles and the increase in our national debt make it very

difficult to cope with the problem or to get any permanent solution. I think we are simply aggravating the situation.
When we look at the estimates presented to the house this afternoon we find a tremendous decrease in all expenditures for the ensuing year. There are one or two cases where increases have been made, however. One case is the interest on the national debt, which has been increased by about $13,000,000. Another case of an increase is the estimates for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which have gone up approximately $500,000. That is where our money goes, and I want to say that w'hen we start to economize on wages we are starting at the wrong end. We should do something about those tremendous interest charges, and I think if we did so we would be doing a good thing for Canada.
I was very much disappointed in the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). I had hoped that on an occasion such as this, when we are having our first discussion of this important problem of unemployment, at least the minister would have told this house and the hundreds of thousands of men and women out of work what the government intend to do, but in his remarks there was not one word or one syllable which would give a ray of hope in this connection. I am very sorry that this was so; I am sorry the government have taken that attitude. I was looking for some constructive proposal, some word as to what the government intend doing during the coming year in order to deal with this extremely difficult and, I might add, menacing situation.
We have been told of the great increase in the prosperity of the workers; we have heard of the homes they own, of the electric lights they possess, of the radios, the washing machines and other articles found in their homes. Most of these articles in the average homes are purchased on the instalment plan, and many of them are not paid for. When we talk of the working people owning their homes we forget that in most cases there are very big mortgages on them. But may I give a little information which came to me only a day or two ago in order to show the conditions which exist in some homes. This information was contained in a letter from a very authentic source. It is expected that in the city of Winnipeg in the near future 1,500 children will be born in homes where there is hardly a rag in the house with which to clothe them. That is an actual situation, yet our Minister of Labour speaks about building up a strong nation. There is no one in this

house who more earnestly desires that end to be brought about than the members representing the Labour party, but when children are bom under the conditions I have just described, I ask: what chance have they of growing up into decent, strong, vigorous Canadian men and women? Their chances are very slim indeed.
Some people were surprised that I should introduce a resolution of this kind; they asked what good it would do the farmer. I am free to admit that offhand I cannot say how this is going to affect the farmer; I do not know whether it will be a detriment or a help to him. But if the farmer to-day has nothing but a load of debt, as I am told by farmer members of this house, I do not see how this resolution could affect him in any harmful way at all. On the other hand, if it has the effect of increasing the purchasing power of the great masses of the people, it might be of some benefit to the farmer in this country as well.
I believe I am safe in saying that in introducing this resolution I am voicing the opinions of every shade of labour thought in Canada. There is hardly a labour organization in this country that has not gone on record as being in favour of a shorter working day, and at the same time requesting an increase in their purchasing power. Within the last few weeks a delegation from the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the largest body of organized labour in this country, waited on the government with a memorandum which included a request for a six hour day. That request has been made now for quite a number of years past. Under these circumstances, therefore, when, as I feel, I am speaking here to-night for practically the whole of organized and the great part of unorganized labour in the country, I regret that I cannot see my wa3r to withdraw the resolution. I believe that within the confines of the resolution are contained the very things that are vital so far as the workers are concerned.
And now may I make one reference to a statement made by the Minister of Labour to-day. He stated something about a member of this house, interested in labour questions, having received 369 permits-I believe that was the number he gave-to enable persons to go on farms, those persons having ultimately found their way to the cities. I believe that was the statement he made, and the natural inference was left that I, having brought this question up to-day, was the member who had asked for these 369 permits. I

speechtext:
Very well; it is immaterial to me and I will discuss it as it stands. I move this resolution to-night because in my opinion the present rates of exchange are detrimental to our trade. High rates of exchange between countries have prevented us from trading both within and outside Canada, and if we are forced to trade within the empire then this can be done only by the stabilization of currency within the empire and the abolition of adverse rates of exchange. Personally I cannot see that there is anything new in our trading within the empire, nor in the empire becoming an economic unit. The policy of the Liberal party has always been to trade with the empire and the whole world, and we know that from 1921 up to 1930 Canada was trading with every nation. But even then we did not find that we had a great sur-. plus of markets for our products and we were looking for wider markets with a view to expanding our trade. I am pleased to say, and I think every hon. member will agree with me in this, that during that time our trade went forward by leaps and bounds. Our friends opposite are now advancing the slogan about trading within the empire and making the British empire an economic unit, and I contend that if we are to be forced into the position of trading only within the empire, then the depreciation of the pound sterling, with its attendant disadvantages, makes it almost impossible for us to trade satisfactorily, especially with Great Britain, or with the empire as a whole.
I know that this is a very complicated question and one that has received the attention of leading economists and financial experts throughout the world, and if something can be done to improve the present very unsatisfactory situation every effort should be made in that direction. We are in fairly good company, it seems to me, when we propose this
212	COMMONS
Stabilization of Currency-Mr. MacLean
question in regard to empire currency. I believe that Lord Milner and Lord Beaver-brook were both in favour of empire currency, for in 1917 Lord Milner said:
I believe it to be of the utmost importance to the future of the empire that there should be empire currency.
Some people, including members of this house, are of the opinion that this does not go far enough; they think that an effort should be made to Stabilize the currency of the world and thus do away with unfavourable rates of exchange. I admit that this is quite desirable from every point of view, but at the same time the resolution now before the house is a large order for the time being, and if we could accomplish what is aimed at in this proposal we might then be in a position to say to the rest of the world, "Here is an example which you might well follow". Some people may contend that no hardship is imposed on anyone by present rates of exchange and that in the long run things equalize themselves, so that no one suffers very much from an adverse rate of exchange between one country and another. There may be some truth in that, taking the country as a whole, but that argument will not hold good in the case of the individual, because the individual is likely to be trading one way. He is selling his product to a country that has a depreciated currency, and there is no possibility of his getting any compensation in return. If he were able to sell part of his products in a country with a depreciated currency and the other -part in a country like the United States, where their currency is at a premium at the present time, there might be something in the argument. He might then even things up in the long run. But we know our producers throughout Canada are forced to sell a great many of their products on the British market; they are selling them on a depreciated currency, and there is no way out; they have to take their loss.
Some will say that this currency question is altogether one that is connected with the gold standard, and that we must adhere to it, while, on the other hand, others claim that the gold standard must be discarded. It is not my purpose to-night to discuss the merits or the demerits of the gold standard as a basis of currency, nor do I advocate doing away with the present form of currency in each country. If Great Britain wants to retain her pounds, shillings and pence, I say: let her do so. If Canada, on the other hand, wishes to retain her Canadian dollar, I say: let her do so. But there must be some system under
[Mr MacLean,]
Which the Canadian dollar or the pound sterling will have proportionately the same buying power in any country within the empire, and until we arrive at that point it is going to be pretty difficult for us to trade.
I do not know whether people realize how costly the present system is and how impossible under it it is for us to continue to do business, especially since the present government has adopted a policy of applying the dumping duty on the basis of the currency in the country from which the goods are imported. I have a case in point in a letter that I received from a gentleman the other day, pointing out that as regards the importation of goods from Great Britain, the depreciated currency is taken into account and the dumping duty applied, with the result that there is practically no more free entry of goods, even if they should happen to be on the free list, especially if they are of a class or kind manufactured in Canada. Under date of October 21st last, this gentleman writes:
On September 1st, Joseph Gundry and Company of Bridport, Great Britain, invoiced and shipped to us a lot of smelt bag nets, used for fisheries. They arrived in Canada some time previous to September 24, as they were rebilled from St. John on that date. Unfortunately the documents did not arrive as soon as the shipment, and when we attempted to clear them from the customs, which was shortly after October 1, the Customs department insisted on collecting as a dumping duty the difference between the depreciated value of the pound, on that date, and its par value. We did not clear them from the customs. The shippers made a draft on us in Canadian currency for the total value of the shipment. Smelt bag nets have always been entered free without any sales tax or duty.
You will notice that instead of getting any advantage by the depreciated value of the pound, we would be paying about $5.30 if we entered the nets to-day. Now the position is that if we are obliged to pay for British goods in Canadian currency and the customs demand a dump on free goods, the dump being the difference between the value of the pound at the time of entry, as compared to its par value, then the 'ower the pound goes the more the goods will cost us. This certainly would absolutely kill importations from Great Britain as we can easily get our supplies from the United States^ and in addition, it does not affect any Canadian industry, as these goods are of a class or kind not manufactured in Canada.
I may say in connection with this matter that these gentlemen put up a deposit of $56 and, as a result, after a great deal of correspondence with the department, the goods were released. But if they were of a class or kind manufactured in Canada, although they were permitted to come in free of duty, still that dump would apply. As I said before, this

Stabilization oj Currency-Mr, MacLean
depreciated currency has everything else trimmed, even the high tariff of our friends opposite, in keeping out goods and eliminating everything from the free list.
There -is one commodity with regard to which this comes right home to the people in Prince Edward Island, namely silver fox pelts, of which we handle a large number through the different organizations in the province. We all know that in Great Britain, London is the big market where the world price for those pelts is set. The moment the English currency depreciated to the extent it did, the silver fox business in this country received the worst setback it ever experienced in its history, because it makes no difference who the gentleman is who is purchasing a silver fox pelt, whether he is from London, England, or New York or Montreal, the first thing he does is to figure off the depreciated currency, and that has to ibe borne by the producer of the pelt. The poor fox rancher who is raising those pelts for sale is the man who has to stand the loss. There is a debatable question there. It is the same as the tariff question. Some will say that the consumer pays the duty or the tariff, while others wild say that the shipper pays it. This is largely a question of supply and demand. If there is a very strong demand on the market for a certain article, it is quite possible that the British buyer would pay the price and absorb the depreciated currency, but when you have a surplus of those products and you have to force them on the British market or on the auction sales in the city of London, it is impossible to think of compelling the buyer over there to pay for those in Canadian currency and absorb the depreciation in the English pound. These are some of the things that come home to us in our everyday business transactions and we feel that some effort should be made to overcome this great handicap under which we are labouring. I know there are some who will scoff at the idea and say that it is impossible, that it cannot be done. But if we read history aright and study the trend of affairs we will see that it has been done before. There has been for the past eighteen years an arrangement between Egypt and Great Britain under which the money of the two countries has been exchanged at par, and Mr. McGeer in an address at Vancouver last fall stated that this exchange of money between the two countries had taken, place for a .period of eighteen years on a pa.r basis with profit to the governments of both countries. So if suoh an arrangement can be carried out successfully between Great Britain and Egypt I do not see what should prevent some similar arrangement being .made between Great Britain and the other countries of the empire.
Our government claim that they have a favourable balance of trade at the present time. We have always been told that trade balances rule our exchange. Well, if Canada has a favourable trade balance at the present time, the question we would like to ask our friends opposite is this: Why is the Canadian dollar at such a discount to-day? I made inquiry at the Royal bank to-day and they told me that the discount on Canadian money was still 15 per cent. But that is almost aside from the question that we are discussing.
I have another letter under my hand Which I think I should read to the house. Although perhaps aside from the question, the situation complained of seems so unfair that I can hardly believe it is true. As hon. gentlemen know, some of our soldier pensioners are living across the line, and one writes to me as follows:
I wonder if you could help me. I have only earned thirty dollars in more than four years. At the present time I am living on eight dollars per week given by the state of Massachusetts. Two months ago I got $9.60 pension. This month I have a cheque for $14.70. Ottawa tells me it is adjustments. It costs 36 per cent loss to cash a cheque here. Banks will not take Canadian cheques.
This is a Dominion government cheque. You would hardly think that it is possible. He goes on:
I have to get these cheques cashed through a store and it costs me $7.20 out of a $20 pension cheque, and I have to wait two weeks for the $12.80.
That throws a little light on the hardships that are imposed on our soldier pensioners across the line. As I said before, you can talk of restricting trade, but there is nothing in the world that will restrict trade to t'he same extent as a depreciated currency. It simply stifles trade, and the result is conditions such as we have to-day. I think that the unemployment situation which our friends have been discussing in the house this afternoon has in part been brought about by just such conditions. It means a loss of markets; it means a loss to the transportation systems; and if our transportation systems are crippled to-day it is 'because our trade has been stifled by a depreciated currency and high tariffs which will not allow commodities to move. It is no wonder that our business men will not venture out into the open and try to do business under such conditions.
There are many other angles to this subject which have been discussed from time to time, such as the reorganization of our banking institutions to conform to the central banking system. That suggestion has been advanced in this house. It has been discussed on many
214	COMMONS
Stabilization nj Currency-Mr. MacLean
occasions here by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and other authorities on this subject. Then tnere is the question of the issue of dominion notes to one-fifth of the banks' deposits. Some advance that as a cure for our present ills. They claim that if we were allowed to issue dominion notes up to one-fifth of the banks' deposits, that would give us somewhere in the vicinity of
8325.000.	000 more notes in circulation. They claim that there were only 8174,000,000 of dominion notes in circulation in 1930 and that this amount could be very well increased by
8325.000.	000, which would still be quite safe and within the recommendations as submitted by the Macmillan commission when they were investigating similar conditions in Great Britain. However, I am not here to advance any of these suggestions as they are no doubt reforms that our people would hesitate to try.
We are labouring under a severe handicap at the present time, and if we can adopt some more workable scheme without endangering or disturbing our present financial arrangements, which have been giving good service to the country, I think we should look into the question and endeavour to bring about some improvement. I have under my hand a work by Mr. J. F. Darling, C.B.E., entitled A New Money to Unify the Empire. If I may be permitted, I should like to read a short extract, as it will place before the country at least one way in Which our present difficulty might be met. He says:
In suggesting a new money unit wherewith to unify the empire, it is not necessary to consider the creation of either a new coin or a currency note which would pass current throughout the empire. Britain, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and the Irish Free State would still retain their pounds each, as, at present, a separate monetary unit; Canada would retain its dollar and India its rupee. In short, with the exception of the gold sovereign where it still circulates, existing currencies in the empire would continue to function practically as they do now.
What is suggested is a new unit which would link up these various currencies by forming a common basis on which each would be issued. This new unit need not be composed of either gold or silver, nor yet of an amalgam of the two metals. It would be found to act more efficiently and economically simply as a "money of account," or, in other words, as the money in which a super-bank of the empire would keep its accounts.
This super-bank could be called the "Bank of the Empire." Its customers would be few, but tremendously important. They would comprise the Bank of England, the government of India, the Canadian government and the noteissuing banks of Canada, the Reserve bank of South Africa, the Commonwealth bank of Australia, the Bank of New Zealand and other note-issuing banks in that dominion, and the

Currency Commission of the Irish Free State. These are the primary issuers of currency in the various parts of the empire. In each case- with the exception of India, where the reserve is largely silver-it is enacted by the respective governments that a given proportion of gold or gold assets should be held against the currency issued. Legislation would therefore require to be passed by each of the governments concerned permitting a balance with the Bank of the Empire to replace gold for all reserve requirements. That is to say, just as a London clearing bank regards its balance with the Bank of England as part of its cash reserve, so would the Bank of England itself regard its balance with the Bank of the Empire; and the same would apply to the other note-issuing banks and governments.
A most appropriate name for this new imperial money would be the "rex." The rex would be created for the exclusive use of the Bank of the Empire as the money in which it would keep its accounts.
The Bank of the Empire would be prepared to "buy gold at a fixed minimum price, paying for it in rex by crediting one or other of its few but important customers with the proceeds. It is suggested that this minimum price should be one rex for 113 grains of the fine gold, which is the gold content of the sovereign. The sovereign-the symbol of the pre-war gold standard-would cease to be coined. In place of the right, in countries where such still exists, to take gold to the mint to be coined into sovereigns, there would be substituted the right, which would be extended to all parts of the empire, to take gold to the Bank of the Empire to be paid for in rex-that is to say, in a balance at the Bank of the Empire-at 113 grains of fine gold per rex. The currencyissuing banks and governments, being the only customers of the Bank of the Empire, would act as agents for the bank in the purchase of gold, just as in pre-war days the Bank of England acted for the Royal Mint.
It is important, however, to note that it is the rex. and not the gold, that would become the basis for the currencies of the empire, and that the rex would thus constitute a new standard of value. The full significance of these fundamental changes will be better appreciated at a later stage.
It appears that this gentleman has gone into the matter thoroughly and has submitted, in a very able work which he has published, the suggestion for one bank. as a clearing house for the whole of the British Empire and this new money, the rex, to be used not in the different countries but just in connection with the clearings of this bank.
In the address given by Mr. McGeer at Vancouver on October 30, 1931, I find the following:
What the empire needs is the establishment of the money exchange system now in operation between Egypt and Great Britain for Canada and Great Britain and all other nations which comprise the British Empire (i.e.), a system that has maintained between Great Britain and Egypt, a perfect par exchange for over 18 years, at a profit to both governments.

Stabilization of Cwrency'

Mr. Rhodes
Another splendid work on the stabilization of the dollar is one by Fisher, but I shall not take the time of the house to read it.
I should be the last one, Mr. Speaker, to suggest any move which would in any way disturb the present financial structure of our Canadian banking system or, for that matter, the banking system of Great Britain as a whole. Our Canadian banks have given wonderful service. They have stood the strain and stress of difficult times, and, generally speaking, the people's savings, with very few exceptions, have been safe in them. Today, however, we see a different situation looming on the horizon, and it may be that some way will have to be found to meet the conditions with which we are confronted. As Mr. McGeer stated:
Six months ago Canada was concerned about the man who was unemployed; those people who had property and business and interest bearing securities were not worrying. But to-day the saleability and negotiability and the shrinkage in market values of these securities have now changed the situation.
We do not know what the future has in store for us. I submit, however, that at the coming Imperial conference this question should be thoroughly discussed. I know we will hear from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and other leading economists in this house, hon. gentlemen who have made a study of finance, and I believe if something could be arranged to remedy the present situation and do away with some of the disabilities under which we are labouring, a great good would be effected. To my mind the time is ripe for the consideration of this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I think I should say a word rather than have the motion disposed of with only the remarks of the mover (Mr. MacLean) before us. Perhaps the very silence in the house following the speech of the hon. member who moved the resolution bears eloquent testimony to the fact that there are not very many who are prepared to jump into a consideration of the question put forward by my hon. friend from Prince. The fact that there appeared to be no desire on the part of any hon. member to speak would seem to bear witness to the truth of the statement my hon. friend made at the outset of his remarks, to the effect that the subject is highly complicated. With all respect to him may I say that I do not quarrel with his initial statement to the effect that he was dealing with a subject with respect to which he knew very little. In fact, Mr. Speaker, if
I may say so again with respect, as he proceeded with his remarks I was reminded of the comment of Mark Twain that everybody complains about the weather but nobody seems to do anything about it. With all deference to my hon. friend I agree that he has propounded a very serious and important question, but, with further deference, I cannot say that he has contributed anything to the elucidation of it.
Having been Minister of Finance for some twelve days I bring to the subject all that wealth of wisdom, assurance and knowledge which is possessed only by extreme youth. Consequently I never expect to know so much about finance or subjects of exchange and empire currency as I do at the present time. Notwithstanding that wealth of knowledge which I now possess, as a youthful Minister of Finance may I say to my hon. friend that I find this subject almost as baffling as, apparently, he does. At the outset of my hon. friend's resolution I find the expression: "if the empire is to become an economic unit." In other words he predicates his resolution upon the assumption, I take it, that the empire should become an economic unit.

I do not know the interpretation my hon. friend vishes to place upon that first paragraph. I submit that he said not one word with respect to that part of the resolution, which to my mind is a rather striking omission. If it bears the importance in the resolution which one might naturally expect, having been drafted with the care and deliberation my hon. friend must have given to it, one might have expected at least some mention of it.
The burden of my hon. friend's remarks consisted of a complaint as to the handicap under which we in this country labour as a result of our unfavourable exchange position as compared with the neighbouring republic, the United States. He instanced the fact that his worthy constituents in the province of Prince Edward Island have suffered because they have to sell their black fox pelts at a lower price than they would have received had there been parity of exchange between the United States and Canada. He also instanced the rather pathetic case-with which we could all sympathize-of the returned soldier who receives his pension in Canadian funds and has to cash his cheque in the United States. But, Mr. Speaker, those two cases have nothing whatever to do with the subject matter of the resolution of my hon. friend. Even if a parity of empire currency
216	COMMONS
Stabilization of Currency-Mr. Rhodes
could be brought about, it would have no reference whatever to the exchange of countries other than those within the empire.
This subject is not new. As a matter of fact in the course of the afternoon I chanced to come across a pamphlet containing a report on Empire Monetary and Financial Policy by a joint committee of the Federation of British Industries and the Empire Economic Union. That committee consisted of some very eminent men indeed. For example the Empire Economic Union was represented by Right Hon. L. S. Amery, M.P., Right Hon. Sir Robert Horne, P.C., G.B.E., K.C., M.P., Sir Basil Blackett, K.C.B., K.C.S.I., and Mr. H. G. Williams, M.Sc., M.I.C.E.; the representatives of the Federation of British Industries were Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, that distinguished Canadian financier, now in England, for many years general manager of the Bank of Montreal, Sir William Larke, K.B.E., Sir Roland Nugent, and Mr. R. G. Glenday. If one cared to peruse this pamphlet he would find at page 20 two or three paragraphs dealing with the very subject brought forward by my honourable friend. But the significant feature is this, that these men whose lives have been largely concerned with finance, banking, exchange and world currency, while they raised the question they offered no solution. Therefore I am sure my hon. friend will not expect me to move too rapidly in offering a solution of this very important question that he has propounded tonight.
And this subject is not new so far as empire conferences are concerned. It was raised at the Imperial economic conference of 1923 at the instance of New Zealand, and certainly the financial wisdom represented on that occasion was unable to offer a solution of the problem other than to suggest that inasmuch as the various countries of the empire were rapidly approaching a gold standard the solution was to be found in that circumstance.
Now, sir, so far as we are concerned-and I think I can speak for the government in this respect-we find no fault with the concluding portion of the hon. gentleman's resolution, namely, that the stabilization of exchange would be of the utmost value in promoting and in continuing inter-empire trade, and I think we are also prepared to agree with him that the subject is of sufficient importance to be included in the agenda of the Imperial Economic conference. Looking at the resolution in that light, I think we can accept it. I can only assure him that this government, as I am confident would be the case if any other government were in office, 
is prepared at the Imperial economic conference to discuss this or any other subject with the purpose of pooling our ideas in order to arrive at a solution that will serve to promote inter-imperial trade.

I did not say what kind of
angel; perhaps my hon. friend would object were I too specific. I may say that I was instructed by my group to put on the order paper a resolution somewhat along these lines. I did so, but through a mistake on my part I lost my favourable position on the order paper, and so take this opportunity to discuss the present resolution.
I think the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) is to be congratulated on his splendid courage, and also for provoking a discussion which should be of very great importance and benefit to this house and even to the government. Although I have no doubt that the government is very wise and well versed in all the mysteries of finance, still I do not think it can ignore a suggestion from the house. So I think this is an opportunity we should embrace, in view of the coming Imperial economic conference, to deal with a subject that is of fundamental significance to the economic difficulties of empire.
So far as the resolution is concerned, I agree with the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in the exception which he took to the fact that stabilization is predicated upon the empire becoming an economic unit. Now, sir, it is rather astonishing that the hon. gentleman who last week indicated that the Colorado beetle had prevented the economic unity of the empire should be the one to bring in a resolution predicated on that very disunity. The mere fact that the Colorado potato bug can upset the unity of the empire is in itself a sufficient reason why the stabilization of currency should not be predicated upon anything of that sort.
I think we will all agree with the importance of the stabilization of currency within the empire, but in my opinion the resolution should have gone a little bit further and made some suggestion as to the probable basis upon which such stabilization should take place. It would be possible to stabilize the currency of an empire or the currency of a nation and make it worse because of its being stabilized.

Stabilization o) Currency-Mr. Irvine
We all appreciate at the moment the necessity for the stabilization of currency, but unless we have some assurance that the basis upon which the stabilization shall take place will be worth while and sound and sane, then we had better not have stabilization at all.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I intend to move an amendment to this resolution, seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), which will set forth the principles on which we believe stabilization should take place. In dealing with this subject perhaps I might be pardoned if I remind the house that the very first speech I made some ten or eleven years ago was on the subject of finance. As the Minister of Finance has just said, sarcastically about himself, I knew more about the subject then than I do now; I am quite willing to admit that; nevertheless I was not entirely ignorant of some of the points in connection with it, although I probably was the only one in the house that believed so at that time. Perhaps I should point out that on that occasion I urged monetary reform, and I think I have urged it every year since I have been here. I urged that Canada should not return to the gold basis but should abandon it, and I predicted, if you please, very much what has come to pass in Canada and in the world since that time with regard to the economic situation. I might add that on that occasion I was laughed at, particularly by the front benchers of that day. One hon. gentleman went so far as to offer to make me king of Canada if I would settle some of the great financial questions with which I had been dealing. That was all very fine, but there is no one in this house who will laugh at what I am going to say to-night, because to do so would expose an ignorance which no hon. member would wish to own.
As I say, I was laughed at by the front benchers on that occasion prior to the last revision of the Bank Act. I had secured the sanction of this parliament to conduct an investigation into the basis, function, and control of financial credit prior to the amendment of the act; I thought it would be wise for us to have a review of the entire financial situation before we approached the revision of the act, and we got that resolution passed through parliament. However, while we spent a good deal of time in that investigation of credit, and while we had some very eminent men give evidence before that committee, the material we obtained was quietly buried. We never heard anything more about it, and the investigation went for practically nothing.
But since that time great events have taken place; a tremendous body of opinion has gathered in favour of financial reform; economic upheavals have swept across the world as a direct result of weaknesses in the financial structure of the world; a tremendous literature on modern finance has piled up in libraries; influential committees throughout the empire have given their views, in no uncertain terms, as to the necessity of the abandonment of the gold standard, the organization of a financial system upon a strictly scientific basis, and the substitution of a managed currency for an unmanaged accident of stupidity known as the gold basis.
