If the right hon. gentleman will permit me to do so I will refer to that under another heading. Probably I will quote fiom the Macmillan report and also from the report referred to by the Minister of Finance dealing with that very point. But for the moment let me say that civilization itself is in imminent danger, largely as the result of a financial policy which I shall characterize as ignorantly conceived, blindly followed and wantonly applied. So we have the condition which is confronting us at present; it could not have been otherwise under the circumstances, and to-day I urge that something fundamentally constructive must be done quickly if disaster is to be averted.
A few years ago, Mr. Speaker, perhaps a generation ago, the governments of the world had a tendency more or less to ignore the economic unity of the world, the interdependence of the various nations in economic matters, but to-day I think there is a tendency to go in the other direction and to say that our problems cannot be solved because they are all international in character. The truth must be found somewhere in between those extremes. I think there can be little doubt that questions of tariff, of disarmament and of finance can be more adequately handled internationally than they can be handled nationally. I believe in respect to tariff that the free traders of to-morrow will have to make their appeal to an international court, because these questions cannot be finally settled by any one nation. An appeal to an international court must be made also in respect to disarmament, and ultimately some international body
218	COMMONS
Stabilization of Currency-Mr. Irvine
will have to settle the question of finance as well. But when that is admitted we have to admit also that the time is so short and the disaster so imminent that we cannot afford to wait until all the nations of the world come to an agreement on matters of finance. I may be wrong in this, but I am assuming that the attitude of mind to be found in the British commonwealth of nations is such as to make some practical advance possible in matters of finance. That being so, we ought to embrace the opportunity which will be afforded by the Imperial conference to discuss these matters and, if possible, make some headway in respect to them; because if we wait until all the other nations of the world, and especially those who have become gold minded, since the war, get ready to assist us, I am afraid we shall have to wait too long.
I have this conviction, Mr. Speaker: that there is sufficient intelligence and good will in the British empire to reconstruct our own financial system on a sound, proper basis. If other nations wish to drown themselves with golden millstones around their necks, let them do it. To find within the confines of the British empire all that is required to maintain the highest possible standard of living in modern times, yet lacking the financial genius to bring these things to the consuming public, would be a bad thing to be said about the statesmanship of the British empire. I hope it will not have to be said; I believe there is a way out, and I believe the Imperial conference will find that way. Canada has had a great deal to do with that Imperial conference; I think Canada will be given a good deal of the credit for it, and perhaps for a good many of the things that will be discussed. I hope Canada will take the lead in this matter also, and that this greatest of all modern questions, the question of finance, will be up for discussion.
I need not emphasize the advantage to Canada and Great Britain at the present time of the stabilization of currency. Briefly stating it, I think the rate of exchange on the pound in Montreal to-day is 83.97, while in New York it is 83.45. This means that on every carload of wheat and every shipment of live stock which the western farmer gets into the British market he loses 90 cents on the English pound. Under present world conditions, and with prices as they are to-day, to add 90 cents to that makes it a disastrous thing indeed, and no doubt our export trade with Great Britain would fall very considerably following the collapse of the pound sterling. So that there is not much use in the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Com-

merce securing better markets in Great Britain for our goods by better tariff arrangements when we find that the difference in exchange nullifies all that they have been able to do. I think it will be admitted even by the government that if w'e could find any way of putting our money more nearly on a parity with that of Great Britain it would be of great advantage in our export trade. I would go so far as to say that we should be better off to-day if our money were stabilized at the value of the British pound.
But, I shall be asked at once, what would happen in the United States? Well, what would happen in the United States? I understand that Canada has been meeting her obligations there so far with gold; I presume that was -what the Prime Minister, when he was Minister of Finance, meant when he said that Canada was still on the gold basis. It meant that we were honouring our obligations internationally by paying in gold. If that is so, the honour would be in no way impaired if our dollar were worth 25 cents less than it is. Moreover, our export trade to the United States would be increased because their money would buy more in Canada than it would anywhere else, and we could find a good market in Great Britain because our money would be on a parity with theirs. I will not spend any more time emphasizing the importance of stabilization of British currency on a parity. All will agree on the advantages, if it could possibly be brought about.
In this connection I want to refer to the report of the joint committee of the Federation of British Industries and the Empire Economic Union, dated October 14, 1931, and perhaps also, if I have time, it might be well for me to refer to the report of the committee on finance and industry usually called the Macmillan report. I shall quote this briefly on certain points which I intend to argue. The committee on economic union, I may observe in passing, was composed of the following:
Sir Basil Blackett, K.C.B., K.C.S.I.
Right Hon. L. S. Amery, M.P.
Right Hon. Sir Robert Horne, M.P.
Mr. H. G. Williams, M.Sc., M.I.C.E.
The members of the Federation of British Industries included Sir Frederick Wiiliams-Taylor. I think that is the same gentleman who was president of the Bankers Association in Canada when there was being considered by a committee of this house a resolution dealing with credit matters. I can truly say, if he is the same gentleman, that he has given his O.K. to almost everything in this

Stabilization of Currency-Mr. Irvine
report which at that time he opposed in that committee. That is not a criticism; indeed,
I am going out of my way to compliment him upon having, during the intervening years, come to a better frame of mind. And I might suggest that if Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor has changed his mind in that time there is no reason why any gentleman in this house should fail to change his in the same time and on the same subject. The other members for the Federation of British Industries are:
Sir William Larke, K.B.E.
Sir Roland Nugent.
Mr. R. G. Glenday.
The next thing I want to refer to is the finding of these economists that the chief cause of the crisis is the monetary system. The committee does not say it is the only cause, and neither do I. But the personnel I have mentioned do hold that the chief cause of' the crisis to-day throughout the world is the breakdown of the monetary system. The report states:
The want of a proper standard of purchasing power is the chief cause of the survival of the monstrous fallacy that there can be too much produced of anything.
We agree with the conclusion of the Macmillan committee that the present world economic crisis is primarily a monetary crisis. And the report further says that the recent unparalleled fall in prices has been due in the main to a shortage of gold. The story of this disastrous deflation which has brought us to the present economic impasse began with the return to the gold basis after the war, Great Britain taking the lead. The Macmillan report mentions this fact as the main part of the explanation of the depression, or what is sometimes called the crisis.
Merely because a committee says that the monetary crisis is the chief cause of our difficulties does not, of course, prove it beyond any possible doubt, and I have no time, seeing that the clock is moving so fast, to argue all the details. I am glad, however, to have such an authority as this committee to quote in this respect, for it saves me much of the argument. Personally I have no doubt about the matter. I believe that in the British countries to-day, not to speak of others-and they are all the same-our monetary system, having up to this time been limited or controlled by the gold standard, in respect to both currency and credit, could not possibly have any real relation to the economic necessities of the case. If necessary I will demonstrate in a few moments just what I mean by that. Gold
is not controllable-and this will answer in part what the Prime Minister asked me- because in the first place you do not know how much of it you can find next week or next year, and therefore it has no relation to the amount of goods which will be in readiness, waiting to be distributed by money, which can be issued only on gold so long as we maintain the gold basis. Next, you have no control of gold because even Great Britain could not prevent other countries from bleeding her white of a commodity of which the empire produces 70 per cent of the entire output of the world. That is what I mean when I say that it is not controllable.
If we can find a means of stabilizing British currency on a basis other than gold, then it will be in control of the nations of the empire concerned and they will not be subject to being bled to death by those who wish to drain them from outside. Furthermore, such a basis would always have an intelligent relation to the requirements of money which would be developed by the natural evolution of the industrial process. I believe that the end in view can be attained by the British commonwealth. I say frankly that I do not think it is possible to do it in any other way.
I do not think we can look forward with any hope of such action being taken internationally in the near future. There exists no international body to-day with either the authority or the intention to handle the financial questions of the world. But there does exist an imperial body; or, if you wish to put it in more modern terms, the nations of the British commonwealth have found a way of getting together to cooperate for their own economic and sentimental interests. These nations have the good will and, I believe, the ability, and certainly they have the necessity,, to take action on this matter, and while it is quite likely that the question cannot be settled by them completely, ignoring all the rest of the world, it can be settled sufficiently well to prevent disaster in the empire. In the hope of a satisfactory arrangement of the empire currency, I would urge that the government at least indicate that it is willing to give consideration to the matter with that hope in view and to assist its consideration before the Imperial conference.
In regard to the empire taking action in this matter, the committee's report to which I have just referred has this to say in respect to gold in a monetary sphere:
An imperial sterling currency, so adjusted as to maintain reasonable price stability for the British Commonwealth, and so powerful as to govern, through the external trade of that
220	COMMONS
Stabilization of Currency-Mr. Irvine
commonwealth, both the value of the metallic medium of exchange and, indirectly, the value of the currencies of the rest of the world,-a pax Britanniea built up out of the present anarchy in the world's monetary affairs.
In another place the report says:
There is no insuperable difficulty in securing the desired end if once its importance is recognized by the governments concerned and the political will to achieve it becomes manifest.
I hold that view; I think the committee was right when it said that, and that is why I am urging to-night that our government should give consideration to this suggestion. Referring to the managed currency, the committee says:
Such management aimed at counteracting the serious economic, social and political effects of price instability, may be a difficult and delicate, but should not be an impossible task. Even if the ideal solution might be attainable only by a degree of international cooperation which is not yet in sight, much can be done by a great and wealthy community like the United Kingdom, and still more by so immensely powerful a group of communities as the British Empire, to shelter its own citizens from the worst effects of world monetary fluctuations and, indeed, to bring those fluctuations under some measure of control. Nor need such a policy of national and imperial monetary control interfere with the endeavours to improve international cooperation in this field.
My next point is that Canada should take the ground that the gold standard should be abandoned. This committee also has the following interesting statement:
The rigid linking up of gold and currency which compels the contraction of domestic credit because some quite fortuitous circumstance, like an American boom or a Paris panic, withdraws our gold, and only enables domestic expansion to take place when the foreign exchanges are favourable, are obvious objections to a system which is no longer required in order to maintain public confidence.
That is not t'he member for Wetaskiwin speaking; that is a committee of notables with numerous letters after their names, whose names I have just read to the house, gentlemen of unimpeachable integrity and of great economic knowledge. They go so far as to say that we do not require any longer to have a metallic basis of any kind to establish public confidence.

permit a question?

speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend said that if
the currency were raised to twice its present

Stabilization of Currency-Mr. Campbell
imount, the price of commodities would increase to an equal degree; therefore a farmer getting twice the amount of currency for the commodities he sells would have to pay twice the amount for what he buys. I ask my hon. friend how that would improve conditions, and how the farmer would profit thereby.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The principal problem
in the world to-day is debts, not merely reparations and war debts but public and private debts as well. My hon. friend from Wetaskiwin explained that. The trouble is that those debts were contracted when currency was at a certain level. The currency has been deflated to a point where the dollar is worth twice as much, and the debt is doubled. A farmer who borrowed money on his farm in 1929 is called upon to-day to pay back two or three times the commodity value of what he borrowed at that time. What we want to do now is to devise some system which will bring us back to the normal price level, and a system whereby we can pay these debts.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is arguing
only in regard to debts, and not in regard to exchange values.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Not entirely. Debts
affect the whole business structure. One of the great impediments to the normal condition of business in the world to-day is the burden of debts, and those debts have been increased tremendously. Debtors have found it impossible to pay because of this deflation.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am very much obliged
for the opportunity of asking the question; I just wished to hear my hon. friend in that connection.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It might not have any effect as between commodities. But when Germany made the arrangements for payment under the Young plan the commodity level then perhaps justified the Germans in undertaking the obligation to pay those amounts. The committee that recently examined the question of those reparations reported that Germany under the changed price level would now be called upon to pay three times the amount she had become originally obligated to pay. That is what we are all suffering from to-day.
Now I wish to point out something that I think is going to have a profound effect upon the whole situation, not merely the stabilization of monetary value within the empire, but throughout the whole world. In the United States they have deflated the dollar until it is a long way below, or above-whichever 
way you want to look at it-the normal gold level. That is to say, in the United States normally they require 40 cents in gold behind every dollar in circulation; to-day they have 80 cents. In other words, they have doubled the amount of gold they actually need behind their circulating mediums. What has been the effect? It means that the standard of measurement of the gold basis has been changed altogether. That, I think, is the reason why Great Britain and many other countries had to go off the gold basis. Canada is really on the normal gold basis to-day, but because the United States have deflated their dollar until it is much more valuable than the normal gold basis, we have not been able to follow them and our dollar is at a discount in New York.
What has happened in the United States? There you have another case of King Midas. The United States with the greatest amount of gold of any nation in the world, their vaults full of gold, found they could not eat their gold, could not make clothes out of it, could not even turn it into useful tools. But coincident with this immense reserve of gold they have the greatest amount of agricultural distress and industrial unemployment that has ever prevailed in their history. Now President Hoover has come out with a scheme which I think will be a partial corrective. A recent newspaper despatch refers to it as one of the greatest inflations in history. A despatch from Washington of February is headed:
Permit Inflation of U.S. Currency
Sensational Rise in Commoditj Prices is Forecast.
Then follows the despatch:
The United States government moved to-day to permit inflation of the American dollar. Senator Carter Glass, Democrat, Virginia, introducing a government measure permitting the Federal Reserve to "make advances to member banks on time, demand, or promissory notes," announced the bill was not for "excessive inflation of currency."
In fact, the bill would permit the federal reserve board to use its surplus stocks of gold -at present the dollar is backed by 80 per cent gold, whereas the legal limit is 40 per cent-to provide currency in exigency.
The first result of the government's move forecast in this morning's papers was a sensational rise in commodity and security prices.
Ogden L. Mills, Secretary of the Treasury, and other government officials, strenuously contended to-day the step should not be called
"inflation" but rather counter-deflation. It is the government theory that prices are too low and that recovery is prevented by the psychology of the country.

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
As I said a moment ago, I think before very long we are going to see the greatest inflation in the history of the United States. That means the United States dollar will go down in value, and probably by the middle of next summer, or before, our Canadian dollar will come back to par in New York. But I would warn any of our Canadian statesmen not to boast of that as a result of their own efforts; it would simply mean that the American dollar has come down to meet the Canadian dollar.
I hope so. It will help to correct some of the evils here. It is more than possible that the American dollar will go down below our own, and in that case I would suggest to the government that they follow the line of the American administration and permit inflation to the same extent. The American dollar may go down to where the British pound will come back to par, in which case it will solve a good many of our international problems. I think the government should carefully watch this and not be too much afraid of what we call "inflation." Inflation, as one newspaper has said, is not the right word. The United States have "dehydrated" their dollar to the point where it is worth more than the normal gold dollar, and now they are only bringing it back to its former value. A few years ago some of us in western Canada were very much exercised over the fact that the terminal elevators were drying out our damp and tough wheat to such a degree that it became a concentrated wheat and more valuable than wheat which normally contains 12 or 13 per cent moisture, and the millers would pay a great deal more for it. We objected to that. The United States authorities have done precisely the same thing with the dollar-they have dried it out, they have dehydrated it to the point where it is more valuable than the normal gold standard value. I hope the government will watch the situation in the United States and try to keep in line with their policy.
On motion of Mr. Spencer the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At this hour, perhaps,
Mr. Speaker, we had better adjourn rather than call the next motion.
It is proposed to-morrow to take government orders, and after that supply-public works, trade and commerce and justice. They will be taken up in this order.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Before the house adjourns, Mr. Speaker, may I direct the attention of my right hon. friend to what I think must be an error on his part, either a very simple one, or as he said a few days ago, one made with malice aforethought, though I do not for one moment indicate that such is the case. At the adjournment of the house Friday last my right hon. friend is reported in Hansard as having said:
As I explained, some of the opposition members desired to be present when bills were read the second time, and they have stood.
I have been unable to find in Hansard any previous reference by my right hon. friend to bills standing, and I do not find that any member of the opposition asked for bills to stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
"Some hon. members,"
without the "opposition" would be the correct statement.

I am very glad of that correction, because as Hansard reads it appears as if some opposition members were responsible for bills not having been proceeded with.
While on my feet, as a matter of privilege, and in order to clear up a misunderstanding, I may perhaps be allowed to refer to the incident that took place the other evening when my right hon. friend mentioned that in my speech at London I had made a statement which was not based on the evidence-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-in reference to his not having permitted a contribution to be accepted from Beauharnois. My right hon friend said that in the evidence it was never suggested by any person that a sum of money had been paid to (he federal Conservative party by Beauharnois. I had not the evidence at hand at the time the Prime Minister spoke, but I felt perfectly sure that the statement I had made was based on the evidence. I have since looked up the evidence, and my right hon. friend will find it in the Journals of the House of Commons, Canada, volume LXIX, 1931, appendix No. 5, page 822. Mr. Sweezey was giving his evidence, and Mr. White was questioning him. These are the questions and answers:
Q. And then who else if anybody?
A. Well, still speaking of federal campaign funds, I do not recall of any specific-oh, yes, I



Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
contributed to General McCuaig, who, I understood, was the collector for the Conservative campaign fund in Montreal.
Q. How much?

Q. Anybody else?
Mr. Lennox: You did not treat us very generously.
Then a little later on the same day he said:
Q. Have you told us all of the federal contributions ?
A. Yes, sir.
I submit that the reference there is to federal contributions, and that there is a direct statement made by Mr. Sweezey that he made contributions to the collector for the Conservative campaign fund in Montreal, indicating that he had in mind that he was the collector for the federal party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no such reference. It says "in Montreal."
The reference is very clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not.

As my right hon. friend says, we are in the judgment of our peers. The answer is:
A. Well, still speaking of federal campaign funds. . . .
Those are Mr. Sweezey's words.
... .1 do not recall of any specific-oh, yes, I contributed to General McCuaig, who, I understood, was the collector for the Conservative campaign fund in Montreal.
Then a Conservative member on the committee, Mr. Lennox, speaking to Mr. Sweezey, is reported to have said:
You did not treat us very generously.
The word "us" must have meant the federal party. Those were the references I had before me when I made the statement that the contribution had been made to the federal fund. Certainly I was not trying to do the Prime Minister an injustice as to his having returned any contribution; I was making the point that he had returned it. My point was that the reason he did so was not that it was in the public interest so to do, but that he expected to have an investigation and therefore was not going to accept any funds in the interval, which did not seem to me too exalted a reason.
Now may I just say to my right hon. friend that I do not think I am any more inclined to do things with malice aforethought than he is, nor do I think I am given to making statements about other people with a view to doing them deliberate injury.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is nat a question
of privilege at the moment.

My right hon. friend may stop me if he wishes to do so. I say that in view of the statement I have given to the house as to the basis of my remarks, his statement that I had made a statement which was false or which I should have known was false and was therefore wilfully negligent in the discharge of my duty, was wholly uncalled for and unworthy of him. I have just pointed out where, at the close of the session on Friday, he made the deliberate statement that the opposition had been responsible for certain bills not being gone on with. He now says he did not say anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that. If it is in Hansard I must have used the words.

My right hon. friend says he did not mean what he said, and I accept his word like a gentleman. I think my right hon. friend might be equally gentlemanly in accepting the word of those who speak from 'this side.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon.
gentleman has raised a question of privilege with which I shall deal at once. His statement at London, Ontario, was with reference to $200,000; it was with reference to General McRae; it was with reference to the treasurei of the Conservative party. The observations just made bring to mind the words of a British statesman with respect to a similar matter. He said, "It is unworthy of any man who calls himself a statesman, and only of a pettifogging attorney." Those were the words used with respect to a similar matter. Every member of this house knows what was said last year; my right hon. friend knows what the evidence shows, and I will take occasion to Tead the statement he made at London and compare it with what he now says. Then I hope he will make the amende honorable to this house, 'the members of whom are his judges. Then he will not stand here and endeavour to divest himself of responsibility for what he said at London with reference to a matter which was not at all the subject matter of his address on that occasion.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.55 pun.
